families.name: Content
families.def: What information each component shows, and how it is abstracted from the underlying item: visually, semantically or computationally.
families.q: What is shown where, and in what form?

families.name: Composition
families.def: How multiple instances and components relate: cardinality, nesting, recursion, linking and synchronization.

families.name: Layout
families.def: The spatial arrangement of components, and of items inside them.

families.name: Invocation
families.def: How a component is summoned and dismissed: the trigger, the entry point, and the way back.
families.q: What brings it up, and from where?
families.origin: Meridian openBy / openFrom; the Click, Hover and Back annotations in CHI '25 Fig. 3; study participant P6

families.name: Flow
families.def: Progression through steps or states: linear, branching, free or resumable, and the rules for moving between them.
families.q: In what order, and under what rules?

families.name: Lifecycle
families.def: Time-bound behaviour: when something appears, how long it persists, how it expires and how it updates live.
families.q: When does it appear, change and go away?

families.name: Initiative
families.def: Who acts: the person, the system or an AI, and how control is handed between them.
families.q: Who decides, and who does the work?
families.origin: Generalized; anticipated by AI-assisted Fluid Attributes (CHI '25 §4.1.3)

families.name: Feedback
families.def: How state, progress, validation, consequence and error are expressed back to the person.
families.q: How does the person know what happened?

families.name: Scope
families.def: The unit an operation or attribute applies to: an item, a selection, a group, a whole collection, or everything.
families.origin: CHI '25 study: participants P6, P10 and P12 wanted attributes about the whole collection, not only each item

families.name: Encoding
families.def: How values map to visual variables and marks: position, size, colour, shape, motion.
families.origin: Generalized from CHI '25 Fig. 11, where attributes invoke a representation (scatter plot, colour space)

families.name: Collaboration
families.def: Presence, authorship, permission and concurrency when more than one person touches the same thing.
families.q: Who else is here, and what may they do?

families.name: Adaptation
families.def: How the pattern changes with density, screen size, platform, input modality or the person’s ability.
families.q: How does it change with context?
families.origin: Generalized from the CHI '25 mobile application (§5.1.5) and Meridian’s responsive-spec discussion (§7)

levels.name: Archetype
levels.def: A user activity broad enough that its design space is abstract: the choices any interface for that activity must make, before it is any particular pattern.

levels.name: Pattern
levels.def: A screen- or flow-level arrangement of components that recurs across products and domains. Overview–detail is the anchor pattern.

levels.name: Component
levels.def: A widget-level unit reused inside many patterns. Its design space is narrow, and its variations often appear as the values of a pattern’s dimension.

archetypes.name: Browse collections
archetypes.def: Scan many things, narrow to the relevant few, and focus on one.
archetypes.q: How is a collection organized, narrowed and focused?

archetypes.name: Navigate and wayfind
archetypes.def: Know where you are, where you can go, and get there.
archetypes.q: How are places structured, shown and traversed?

archetypes.name: Search and discover
archetypes.def: Express what you want, or be shown what you might want.
archetypes.q: How is intent expressed and how are candidates returned?

archetypes.name: Enter and edit data
archetypes.def: Give a system structured information and correct it.
archetypes.q: How is input structured, constrained and validated?

archetypes.name: Create and compose
archetypes.def: Make an artifact by directly manipulating its parts.
archetypes.q: How are objects represented, selected and transformed?

archetypes.name: Communicate
archetypes.def: Exchange messages with people over time.
archetypes.q: How are messages organized, composed and threaded?

archetypes.name: Monitor and get notified
archetypes.def: Keep track of changing state and be interrupted only when it matters.
archetypes.q: What is watched, how is change surfaced, and when?

archetypes.name: Guide and onboard
archetypes.def: Learn a system while using it.
archetypes.q: When, where and how does help appear?

archetypes.name: Transact and commit
archetypes.def: Make a consequential choice, commit to it, and be able to take it back.
archetypes.q: How are options compared, confirmed and reversed?

archetypes.name: Plan in time
archetypes.def: Arrange things along time and coordinate availability with others.
archetypes.q: How is time represented, and how are things placed in it?

archetypes.name: Explore space
archetypes.def: Understand, navigate and select within a spatial world.
archetypes.q: How is space projected, navigated and annotated?

archetypes.name: Consume media
archetypes.def: Watch, listen or read with control over pace, position and what comes next.
archetypes.q: How are playback, position and queue controlled?

archetypes.name: Configure and personalize
archetypes.def: Change how a system or a product behaves or looks.
archetypes.q: How are options organized, previewed and applied?

archetypes.name: Analyze and visualize
archetypes.def: Find structure in data through representations of it.
archetypes.q: How is data encoded, linked and interrogated?

archetypes.name: Collaborate
archetypes.def: Work on shared artifacts with others, at the same time or over time.
archetypes.q: How are other people, their changes and their permissions made visible?

archetypes.name: Delegate to AI
archetypes.def: Hand a model a goal, then steer, verify and accept its work.
archetypes.q: How is intent handed off, progress shown and output verified?

fable: Initiative has no value for fixed editorial/consumer views where the reader only interrogates (coded n/a); Linkage's Sequential drill was used for tabs and click-through pages that replace the view.

initiative has no value for authored editorial and consumer views (adopted +Fixed authored view) and interrogation has none for typed code or query text (adopted +Write a query). linkage has no value for tabs that swap encodings over one series, so Sequential drill is stretched to cover them, and a news page that both links its views and drills on click needs pick any. encoding's Text and number is read three ways across raters: tables, headline number cards, and hover readouts; the gloss should say the first two and exclude the third. Recommended encodings and Automated insights differ on whether the person chose the fields first, and the gloss does not say so.
opus: Analytical initiative assumes the person analysing is also the person building, which is false for a quarter of the sample (see +Fixed authored view), and interrogation assumes direct manipulation of marks, which misses query editing (+Write a query). Linkage was the judgement call: I read Coordinated multiple views as requiring a real shared selection or time range, so tabbed alternatives (GA4, Our World in Data) stay Single view.

Two codebook faults drove most of this packet. Coordinated multiple views is named for any shared state but glossed only as 'Brushing and linking', while Sequential drill is glossed as 'replace one view with another' and named for drilling — so a tabbed explorer and a parameter-linked graphic land wherever a rater weights name over gloss. And Text and number was read by three raters as three different things: I now take it as a persistent table, card or crosstab, never a legend or hover readout of another encoding.
sonnet: Initiative had no honest fit for fixed, non-configurable personal-analytics screens (Apple Health, Strava, Robinhood, the NYT graphic) — the reader interrogates but never builds, recommends, automates or converses; coded '?' rather than force one of the four.

The initiative sub has no honest fit for fixed editorial/consumer analytics screens where the reader never builds, is recommended nothing, gets no automated insight and can't converse -- proposing +Fixed authored view; interrogation likewise has no value for asking a question by writing/editing free code or a query language rather than working a filter or parameter control -- proposing +Write a query.

Reflow for narrow screens: The New York Times — Covid cases chart

fable: Scale is a pick-one that conflates the x and value axes (time-series with log toggles coded Time); Adaptation's Fixed desktop chart also had to cover fixed mobile encodings.

scale is a pick one across two axes, so every bar, line-over-categories and log-toggle chart holds two values; it wants to be pick any or one sub per axis. adaptation's Fixed desktop chart has to hold every phone-native chart, and has no value for a fixed encoding that resizes with its container. annotation needs a rule that value and legend labels are not callouts, and a reference-mark value for a dot at a value. faceting's Small multiples and a band axis of repeated marks get confused when each category is drawn as its own row.
opus: Scale is pick-one over a chart that has two axes and often a log toggle, so the code records the axis that defines the chart and loses the other. Fixed desktop chart is also doing duty for every chart that simply does not adapt, including five built for phones, and Datawrapper (16) shows the limit of the sample: a generic embed does not fix a mark type, so mark and scale are honestly unknowable.

Three faults did most of the work here. `scale` and `faceting` each want two codes: a chart has a category axis and a value axis (Sheets, GitHub) and the codebook makes you choose one, and clustered/grouped series have no variation at all since Layered series means overlay. `adaptation`'s first variation is named 'Fixed desktop chart', so every non-adapting phone chart in the sample has to be coded as a desktop one. And `annotation` needs the line the raters kept drawing by hand: a data label or a direct series label is furniture, a reference value or a dated note is an annotation.
sonnet: markType/channels/scale were genuinely unknowable for the generic Datawrapper instance since the sample doesn't name a chart type; coded '?'. Otherwise mark type was usually clear from the product description.

The adaptation sub's 'Fixed desktop chart' is a misleading name for what's really 'doesn't restructure across viewport widths' -- it covers native single-context mobile app charts just as much as classic desktop BI, and I initially conflated 'renders on a phone' with 'reflows for narrow screens' across several cells before correcting it.

fable: Trigger lacks a camera move, which is how every map-plus-list product coordinates; Scope is a pick-one over products that mix one-mark clicks with dashboard-wide controls, coded the characteristic act.

scope mixes the unit selected (one mark, a group, a brushed subset) with the reach of propagation (all linked views, one view only), so every click-to-filter dashboard holds two values; it wants to be two subs or pick any. trigger lacks a camera move, which every map-plus-list product uses (adopted +Pan or zoom the view). authorship depends on whether the sample names the editor or the viewer of the same product, and the codebook does not say which to code.
opus: Scope mixes two questions — how big the selection is (one mark, a brush, a category) and how far it propagates (all views, one view) — so an instance where clicking one bar filters every view cannot be coded on both counts; I coded the propagation where the product's point is reach and the granularity where the product's point is marking. Authorship also depends on who is looking rather than on the artifact: the same Kibana or Superset dashboard is fixed for a reader and editable for its author.

`scope` is the codebook fault behind a third of this packet: it mixes the extent of a selection (one mark, a brushed subset, a categorical group) with how far the action reaches (all linked views, one view only), and both are true of every dashboard — it should be two sub-dimensions, or pick any. Second, `linkChannel` has no way to say that a control narrows a single view rather than linking two, which is what split Flightradar24 and Google Trends.
sonnet: Map-pan interactions (Zillow, Airbnb, Google Flights) don't map cleanly onto any listed trigger — closest is Brush a region, since panning redefines a spatial region of interest.

Scope conflates two axes that don't always point the same way: what was selected (one mark / a brushed subset / a categorical group) versus how far the coordination reaches (one view only / all linked views) -- Spotfire's free-form lasso needed the first axis named even though it also reaches every view, unlike the click-based dashboards where the reach was the more informative fact.

entries.name: Focus + context
entries.definition: A detailed focus region shown inside a continuously visible surrounding context in the same visual field—unlike overview–detail, which separates an overview of many items from a distinct detail view of one selected item.

anatomy.name: Lens or distortion
anatomy.role: How focus is carved from context

dimensions.name: Focus–context relation

values.name: Inset mini-map with live focus
values.description: Small context map, large focus—still one navigational act

values.name: Salience-only focus
values.description: Focus is carved out by contrast rather than geometry — the attended region brightens or the rest dims while every element keeps its size and place; the XR and attention-aware case

dimensions.name: Spatial arrangement
dimensions.question: How are focus and context laid out in the field?

values.name: Edge-aware focus panel
values.description: Focus dominates; context as a strip

values.name: Whole-field zoom
values.description: There is no separate focus region: the entire viewport is the focus and the context is whatever remains visible around its edges, reached by zooming the one space; every zoomable map, canvas and globe works this way and none of the five arrangements describes it

values.name: Whole-view zoom
values.description: The entire viewport zooms in and out with no separate lens, inset or fisheye distortion — a plain zoomable map/canvas/graph

dimensions.name: Moving the focus
dimensions.question: How does the focus region move or resize?

dimensions.name: What densifies in focus
dimensions.question: What extra information appears inside the focus?

values.name: Hidden context declutter
values.description: Context shows less while focus shows more

dimensions.name: Degree of interest
dimensions.question: What determines what stays detailed versus compressed?

dimensions.name: Orientation feedback
dimensions.question: How does a person stay oriented while focused?

values.name: Lost without leaving
values.description: Must jump to a separate detail page

wild.note: Authors set lens behaviour; end users rarely retune distortion or DOI functions.

techniques.name: Keep context in frame
techniques.how: Prefer embedded magnification or distortion over navigating away to a separate detail surface when spatial situation matters.

techniques.name: DOI as a visible lens
techniques.how: Expose the degree-of-interest function (pointer, selection, search) as a controllable lens mode rather than a hidden heuristic.

techniques.name: Focus on what answers…
techniques.how: A question moves and densifies the focus region while context stays visible, instead of opening a disconnected detail view.

entries.sample: Maps, graph browsers, creative canvases and code editors that keep surroundings visible while detailing a region.
entries.unit: One focus region inside one continuous context field.
usage: People lose place when detail replaces the overview; focus+context is chosen when orientation matters
questions: When does an inset mini-map still count as focus+context versus collapsing into overview–detail?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Spatial arrangement has no value for whole-field semantic zoom (maps, canvases), coded n/a for seven instances; Relation has none for attention-based dimming (Vision Pro).

arrangement has no value for whole-field semantic zoom, which is a third of the sample (adopted +Whole-field zoom), and relation none for focus by contrast (adopted +Salience-only focus). interest's Uniform zoom doubles as the no-DOI bucket for minimaps where nothing scales, and has no value for a placed lens. focusContent's Geometric magnification only is exclusive by its wording and Extra labels and Hidden context declutter describe one level-of-detail rule from two sides. Pointer-driven fisheye conflates the driver with the warp, so pointer-tracking lenses have no clean value.
opus: Arrangement assumed a lens, an inset or a panel, so the largest family in the sample — plain zoomable spaces — had nowhere to go (see +Whole-field zoom). Interest is also nearly constant: only Gephi has a real degree-of-interest function, and Uniform zoom ends up meaning "no DOI at all", which makes it the default rather than a finding.

Three faults. `arrangement` had no value for the commonest case in the sample — a whole viewport that zooms — so a third of the entry went to n/a or a proposal; two raters proposed it independently and it should be adopted (I have taken sonnet's name). `focusContent`'s first variation is named 'Geometric magnification only', which makes it illegal to combine in a pick-any list, and it records only the focus even where the product densifies the context instead (Xcode). And `moveBy`'s 'Pointer-driven fisheye' welds a mechanism to a distortion, which is why a plain pointer-following lens landed in three different places.
sonnet: Plain 'zoom the whole view' interactions (Maps, Figma, Miro, Google Earth, Gephi, Prezi) are semantic zoom in relation but have no arrangement among the five listed, since all five presuppose a lens/inset/fisheye/XR structure distinct from the base view — proposed +Whole-view zoom.

Arrangement/relation had no value for a screen where the whole field zooms uniformly with nothing carved into a separate focus -- filled by +Whole-field zoom and +Salience-only focus; separately, focusContent's 'Geometric magnification only' is logically incompatible with also picking any other value in the same pick-any list, since 'only' claims exclusivity -- a design flaw when the sub allows multiple selections (this drove several of my corrections on Premiere/Ableton/ArcGIS).

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Execution is a pick-one over products that run selected cells interactively and top-down for versions/jobs; coded the editing flow except where the sample named the batch run (Kaggle).

execution is a pick one over products that run cells singly while editing and top-down or on a schedule as a job; where the sampler names the job I now code it, but the sub wants pick any. deps files Parameterized notebooks, an input model, beside cell-order models. layout cannot hold a notebook that edits linearly and runs as an app, or one with inline chunk output and a rendered preview beside it. assistance's None is read by one rater as no AI, which makes Autocomplete and docs the swing value in every cell.
opus: Deps and execution restate each other for most instances (reactive graph implies reactive recompute, top-to-bottom implies run selected), so the two only carry separate information for scheduled and parameterized notebooks. Playgrounds and live scripts (20, 12) fit the cell vocabulary badly: their unit is a line or a section, not a cell.

The packet here is mostly one rater coding only what the sample note mentioned — assistance came back as None for sixteen products that all ship completion — rather than a codebook fault. Where the codebook is at fault: `deps` mixes a dependency model (order, reactive) with an invocation mode (run selection, parameterized), and `layout` makes an authoring layout compete with App or dashboard mode, which most of these products have as well as, not instead of, a linear scroll.
sonnet: Assistance was 'None' for most notebooks — generative help is still the exception rather than the default even in 2026's mainstream data-science tools, aside from Colab/VS Code's completions.

Most of this entry's disagreement was my own under-coding, not a codebook gap: I marked 'assistance' None for nearly every product despite my own notes naming autocomplete, AI generation or error-fix features (Autocomplete and docs is even the codebook's own named JupyterLab example), and I left several pick-any output/feedback lists too short against evidence already in my notes. The one real interpretive question: for tools with both an interactive 'Notebook' screen and a separate scheduled/parameterized-job feature (Databricks, Deepnote, Snowflake), execution/deps/layout should describe what's on the literally-sampled screen, not the tool's most distinguishing capability reached elsewhere.

entries.unit: One pivot configuration over one fact table or cube.
usage: Analysts pivot axes to answer a new question instead of writing a new query
questions: How should conflicting aggregate semantics be explained when multiple measures share a cell?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Cell display coded as the default rendering (Number only) even where the tool offers heat colours, except pandas where the sample names the styling; Authorship is Person builds the pivot for all twenty.

cellDisplay is a pick one over products that offer plain numbers and conditional colour as options; the sampler's naming the colouring is what I now code, and the sub wants pick any. binding's Flat row and column fields is true of every pivot with one field per axis, so it overlaps Hierarchical nesting and carries no information as a pick-any item. authorship and refresh both depend on whether the sample means the builder or a person running the saved object.
opus: Aggregate is pick-one over a pivot that usually carries several measures with different functions, so the code records the default or headline one; Ask for a crosstab went unused, since natural-language pivot building is not the way any of these twenty are actually driven. Authorship also depends on the reader — a Salesforce matrix report or a published Superset chart is built by one person and run by another.

`cellDisplay` is the fault behind a fifth of this packet: it is pick one, its first variation is named 'Number only', and every BI product in the sample shows numbers with optional conditional colour — so a rater who codes the default and a rater who codes the sampled screen can never agree. `drill` mixes operations that coexist (expand in place vs replace a level) with scoping ones (slice, keep only), which is why Expand hierarchy and Drill down one level kept swapping places.
sonnet: Aggregate defaulted to Sum, the near-universal pivot default, except where the product's own semantics point elsewhere (Mixpanel/Amplitude event counts, pandas' mean default).

Binding was systematically under-coded by me the same way notebook's assistance sub was -- calculated fields, multiple measures and swap-axes were often named in my own instance notes but not coded into the pick-any list. One real ambiguity: pill/hierarchy-native tools (Tableau, Power BI, SAP) don't have a meaningfully separate 'flat' mode the way Excel/Sheets do, since a single pill is still drawn from the same always-nestable mechanism -- both other raters consistently dropped 'Flat row and column fields' for those tools and I now think that's right rather than an oversight.

recorded.gloss: Horizontally scrolling strips stacked vertically — the shelf layout of streaming and store home screens, which a Grid does not describe because each row scrolls independently

recorded.gloss: Variable-height tiles packed into columns, e.g. Pinterest — already named in this codebook's own feed entry but missing from browse-collections' own arrangement list

fable: Three gaps: media-only depth (thumbnail mosaics, poster rows, photo libraries), shelves of carousels as an arrangement, and a node-link graph. Portion is only partly observable for services that load more silently (Slack coded ?).

aggregate has an explicit None value, so [] and ['None'] read as a disagreement that is not one; pick-any lists should not carry a None. depth conflates media presence with attribute count, so a thumbnail beside two text lines lands in Summary or Rich preview by taste. Spatial structure and Visual encoding both claim position on a map. arrangement wants to be pick any when multiplicity is Coordinated.
opus: aggregate has a None variation inside a pick-any, so I wrote ["None"] rather than an empty array. depth needed a rung below Summary for pure thumbnail grids, and arrangement had nothing for shelves of horizontal carousels or for node-link graphs. multiplicity assumes one collection per screen; shelf home screens break it. I treated a global search bar that navigates away as not a narrowing mechanism of the collection on screen.

Three codebook faults drove most of this packet: `aggregate` is pick any yet still lists a None variation, so ['None'] and [] are the same code recorded two ways and score as disagreement; `depth`'s Rich preview gloss ('media plus attributes') does not say whether a row-height icon or cover thumbnail counts as media, which is the whole Spotify/App Store split; and `arrangement` is pick one while `multiplicity` admits Coordinated collections, so a map-plus-list screen has two legal arrangements and no way to record both. Smaller: Grouped does not say whether the buckets must be visible at once (Gmail tabs), and the archetype's `arrangement` and the feed entry's `layout` name overlapping things at different grain (Masonry).
sonnet: aggregate and narrowing are coded from full product knowledge of what the surface supports, not only what the sample's one-line note happens to mention.

Three codebook problems stood out most. (1) Aggregate's 'None' versus an empty list reads as a disagreement to the IRR tooling even when all raters agree nothing aggregates — a representation issue, not a coding one, and it drove roughly a third of this entry's cells. (2) Arrangement is pick-one but Zillow-style coordinated list+map screens truthfully hold two values at once; the codebook's own multiplicity gloss ('Zillow list plus map') already names which one to prefer when this happens, which is a usable tie-break rule the arrangement section itself should state. (3) Masonry is a named variation in the feed archetype's own vocabulary but missing from browse-collections' arrangement list, so the same visual pattern (Pinterest) gets a proposal here and a first-class value there — the two entries' arrangement vocabularies should be reconciled.

fable: Sticky parts is hard to recall from product knowledge for less-visited pages (coded ? on four). Origin needed a variation for third-party compare tools with on-page pickers.

Fixed spec rows versus All attributes is thin because the vendor chose the data fields too; the useful line is hand-curated rows versus the whole schema. Origin's Added from the overview names a mechanism (checkboxes) where the dimension is about who picks, so pickers on the compare page fall outside it; sonnet's +Direct selection and my +Picked on the compare page are one variation. A recommended-plan badge is not any emphasis value. decision's explicit None makes [] and ['None'] a false disagreement.
opus: decision is ['None'] for 19 of 20: outside research prototypes, shipping comparisons compare and stop. emphasis was the hardest sub to apply — the differences control is a small toggle I could not recall for several retail sites, and it is ambiguous whether such a toggle hides identical rows or highlights differing ones. sticky is unobservable without the page in front of you for short tables; I coded [] where the table fits on one screen. A vendor's 'Most popular' plan badge is not Pick a winner, which I read as the person concluding.

The big one: `criteria` reads two ways. 'Fixed spec rows — the vendor chooses' is true of every retail table in a trivial sense (someone defined the schema), so the other two raters coded every spec sheet Fixed and left All attributes with no instances; the useful line is curated shortlist (Apple) versus the whole record rendered (Best Buy, Dell, versus.com), and the gloss should say so. `origin` is really two questions — who assembles the set, and out of what catalogue — which is why two of us independently proposed a variation for 'you pick the items on the comparison tool itself'. `decision`, like `aggregate` elsewhere, is pick any with a None variation, so ['None'] and [] are one code written two ways; and 'Pick a winner' is named as if the person picks, with no room for a site that declares the winner. Finally `emphasis` has no variation for the badged recommended column that every SaaS pricing table ships, which is what pushed sonnet to read those as Highlight the best value.
sonnet: Emphasis is coded '?' rather than guessed where I could not recall a specific product's visual-differentiation behaviour with confidence.

Three codebook problems stood out most. (1) Decision's explicit None versus an empty list caused most of this entry's disagreements (19 of 62 cells) even where all three raters agreed nothing was there — a representation issue, not a coding one. (2) Origin has no value for a dedicated single-purpose compare tool (RTINGS, versus.com, NerdWallet) where items are picked directly rather than checked from a browsed listing; two raters independently invented near-identical variations for it across three instances, which confirms the gap. (3) Emphasis's Highlight the best value doesn't distinguish a vendor's marketing/upsell badge (a SaaS 'Recommended plan') from a genuinely computed value comparison (a benchmark's fastest result or a rate table's lowest APR) — I conflated the two across five pricing-page instances before this round.

fable: Small-screen behaviour is largely unobservable from product knowledge for desktop-first admin tools (coded ? on five). columnSet as pick-one forces Computed over Show and hide when both hold; rowExpansion coded as the prominent capability, not only the default state.

aggregation's Flat reads as an exclusive none, so [] and ['Flat'] and Flat-beside-Pivot are false disagreements; the codebook should say whether Flat excludes the rest. columnSet as pick one forces Computed over Show and hide when both hold. density is MUI's scale and products' own density names do not map onto it. frozen and rowExpansion are coded as offered mechanisms by two raters and as defaults by one; the codebook should say which. smallScreen mixes the web table adapting with a separate mobile app. Tree rows and Grouped rows overlap when a parent row is both an item and an aggregate.
opus: columnSet is two questions in one pick-one: Fixed and Show and hide answer who decides the set, Computed and Generated answer where the values come from. I applied a precedence — Generated > Computed > Show and hide > Fixed — so Airtable, Notion, Sheets and Excel read as Computed columns even though all four also let you hide columns; a rater who read the sub as 'who decides' would code those Show and hide, and this is my likeliest disagreement. density is close to unobservable from memory: most web admin grids sit in a middle band and I coded Compact only for spreadsheet-tight rows. frozen is often a user setting rather than a default, and I coded it where the product is known for it. aggregation has a Flat variation inside a pick-any, so I wrote ['Flat'] rather than an empty array.

Three codebook faults drove most of this packet. (1) columnSet is two questions in one pick-one — Fixed/Show and hide answer who decides the set, Computed/Generated answer where the values come from — so a product with both reads either way; it should be split. (2) aggregation puts Flat inside a pick-any, so 'no aggregation' can be written ['Flat'] or [], and that alone accounts for every aggregation disagreement on the plain admin tables; Flat should be the empty array or the sub should be pick one. (3) frozen and columnSet never say whether to code the default state or the available capability, which is the whole of the Sheets/Excel/Notion split. Two smaller ones: density has no anchor beyond MUI's three names, so raters fall back to Standard as a default; and openIn is pick one where Jira and Airtable truthfully offer a page, a panel and a dialog at once.
sonnet: columnSet distinguishes who controls which fields exist/show; several tools (GitHub Projects, Notion) blur Show-and-hide with letting the person define brand-new custom fields, coded here as Show and hide for lack of a closer fit.

Three codebook problems stood out. (1) Empty list versus explicit 'Flat'/'None' drove a large share of this entry's disagreements even where all three raters agreed on content — the same representation issue as in browse-collections and comparison-table. (2) columnSet is pick-one but Airtable, Google Sheets and Excel all genuinely offer both 'Show and hide' and 'Computed columns' at once (the codebook even cites Airtable as the exemplar for both bullets); I resolved by treating the rarer, more product-defining capability as the diagnostic value, but this should be pick-any or the codebook should state a tie-break. (3) 'frozen' sits ambiguously between a capability list (any available control counts, as I read narrowing elsewhere) and a description of current default state (opus's 'freezing is opt-in so I left it out' reading for Notion) — I ended up applying the capability reading for consistency within this entry, but the two readings produce different codes for Excel, Notion and Google Ads and the codebook should say which one 'pick any' means here.

fable: Position (end state) is hard to know for bounded editorial feeds (Apple News, Google News coded ?). Switchable vs Ranked depends on whether a hidden dropdown counts as a tab; I counted Instagram's.

Switchable and Sort by user overlap whenever the sort keys are exactly ranked and recent, and the codebook should say whether the option set, the control form or a buried setting decides. Headline versus Card preview is undefined for a headline with a thumbnail and no body. Expandable threads needs to say whether always-visible reply previews count. All three raters proposed the same story-cluster nesting under three names, and two proposed the same global-pool source; both are missing values.
opus: ordering forced a call on products whose ranked/chronological switch is a menu rather than tabs (Instagram, LinkedIn): I coded Switchable whenever the switch is reachable from the feed's own header, and Sort by user only where there are several sort keys rather than a pair. nesting is about the feed surface, not the item page, so Reddit's feed is Flat even though the codebook cites Reddit comments — I expect disagreement there. heterogeneity's Uniform posts and Mixed media types are exclusive in practice, so the sub is really one pick-one plus two flags. Whether a given product currently carries ads is the least stable thing here.

Two thirds of this packet is the pick-any problem the brief predicts — one rater's list missing an item the others saw — and it clusters on the sub-dimensions where the feature is intermittent: Injected modules and Ads appear between posts and may not be on screen when you look, and Carousel inside post is a property of some posts and not of the feed. `heterogeneity`, `sources`, `loading` and `nesting` would all score better if the codebook said whether a unit that appears sometimes counts. The codebook faults proper: `ordering`'s Switchable is a special case of Sort by user (LinkedIn's Top/Recent is both by definition), and neither covers an edited feed — Apple News's Top Stories is chosen by people, which Ranked ('an algorithm orders by predicted interest') actively misdescribes. `nesting` has no value for a cluster of several sources' posts under one lead, which all three of us proposed separately. `sources` has no value for an unselected global pool (Hacker News), and its Custom feeds and Lists overlap for a reader like Feedly. `position` has no value for a finite list that never announces its end. And `density` is read two ways — as how much of the body shows (truncation) or as whether the media is whole; the gloss means the former.
sonnet: Several products (Google News, Apple News) blur the line between per-item nesting and page-level sectioning; only Google News's inline related-coverage cluster was coded as nested (+Story cluster), since Apple News's sections are just headers over otherwise standalone cards.

Three codebook problems stood out most. (1) 'sources' undercounts real products more than once: Hacker News's fully unpersonalized global pool has no matching value (hence Global pool), and Apple/Google News's editorial curation isn't 'Ranked' at all (hence Editorially curated) — the ordering vocabulary conflates 'an algorithm predicts interest' with 'a person edits the order,' which are genuinely different mechanisms. (2) Three raters independently invented nearly identical nesting variations (Clustered stories / Clustered coverage / Story cluster) for the same lead-story-plus-related-coverage pattern seen on both Apple News and Google News — a real, recurring gap in the four nesting values, not a one-off. (3) 'Followed accounts' is used inconsistently for topic/community-based sources that aren't personal follows (Reddit communities, Tumblr tags, Feedly boards, Strava clubs) — some of these are closer to 'Topics' than to a social-follow graph, and the boundary between the two values needs a clearer rule than product-by-product judgment calls.

fable: Grouping as pick-one hides that most managers offer By kind and By date as options; I coded the default state and noted the option. Mobile drill-down has no breadcrumbs strictly, coded as the nearest traversal.

metadata does not say whether values shown only in a preview pane for the selected file count; the codebook's own examples are per-row columns, and I coded that way. preview and grouping as pick one need a rule for a toggle that is off by default. A fixed folders-first split and category shortcut locations both get read as By kind by some raters. ownership has no value for a repository or workspace that is shared by construction.
opus: view's List and Details table cannot be told apart from their glosses: the codebook's List exemplar (Finder list view) has named sortable columns, which is also the definition of Details table. I read List as the platform-neutral row list and reserved Details table for the Windows control and its clones, and flagged it. preview conflates 'a rendering of the file' with 'a metadata sidebar'; Box and Dropbox have both, and I coded the rendering. grouping is off by default nearly everywhere, so it is None for 17 of 20 — the three By kind codes are the folders-above-files band in cloud drives, which a rater could reasonably call ordering instead. File pickers (11, 12) inherit the host file manager's view settings, so their codes describe the common case rather than a fixed design.

This entry's disagreements are mostly about *what counts as the screen*, and the codebook is the cause twice over. First, several variations are glossed with a product rather than a screen — Search first is 'e.g., Dropbox home' while the sampled Dropbox instance is All files, and Tree plus content is 'e.g., Windows Explorer' while Finder's sidebar is a places list — so a rater coding the product and a rater coding the screen disagree without either misreading anything. Second, `preview` and `metadata` do not say whether an affordance that must be summoned or switched on counts: Quick Look in an open panel, Explorer's optional preview pane, Total Commander's Ctrl+Q, Nautilus's separately-packaged Sushi, and a details-and-activity sheet behind a menu are all real but none is on screen at rest. I now code the resting state for `preview` and count a per-item pane for `ownership` only if this screen can open it; that rule is mine, not the codebook's. Smaller: `metadata` has no value for a change description (all three of us proposed one, two by the same name), and `ownership` is pick any but has a Local only value, so an empty list, ['Local only'] and n/a all get used for 'none of these'.
sonnet: grouping and view are coded for each screen's default/typical configuration rather than every capability the product exposes; metadata, ownership and other pick-any fields draw on full product knowledge, not only the sample note.

Three patterns stood out. (1) A recurring sidebar-versus-navigation confusion: several products (Finder, the Photoshop/Word open dialogs, GNOME Files) have a sidebar of bookmarked locations that I initially coded as 'Tree plus content,' when the actual traversal mechanism is breadcrumb drill-down; Figma's sidebar, by contrast, genuinely nests Projects under Teams and is a real tree — the codebook doesn't currently distinguish 'sidebar of shortcuts' from 'sidebar that is itself a hierarchy.' (2) 'Preview' repeatedly caught tools where opening a file IS the application's primary edit surface (VS Code, Figma, Canva) — none of that is a file-manager-style preview, and I initially over-coded a 'Viewer page' or 'Preview pane' for several of these before recognizing the pattern. (3) Metadata's 'what shows on the row itself' versus 'what shows in a separate detail/preview panel' is an easy conflation (Finder column view, iOS Files icon grid) that the codebook could make explicit.

recorded.gloss: An open-ended filter builder for arbitrary criteria assembled on the spot, distinct from a one-click saved Quick filter, e.g. Asana's board Filter button

fable: cardFields depends on configuration for most tools; I coded what a typical default card shows. Swimlanes and column source are coded as the sampled screen's default, with the alternative noted.

cardSize's Expanded example names a per-card option, not a board setting. cardFields cannot say a card carries money, which is the point of every CRM board in the sample. columnBehaviour has no value for a phone board that shows one column per screen. Quick filters and Saved views overlap when saved filters sit in a one-click dropdown. Whether paid-tier features count is uncoded and splits raters on GitLab. columns as pick one splits raters between the instance's default grouping and the regroup capability.
opus: columns is ambiguous for products where the grouping attribute is configurable but defaults to status (Linear, ClickUp, Planner): I coded the instance as shown rather than the capability, and said so per instance. transitions mixes enforcement (Allowed transitions only, Required fields) with side effects (Automation on move), and nearly every modern product has some automation, so Free movement plus Automation on move is the default shape. columnSummary's card count is nearly universal and Trello's being opt-in is the only real variation in it. openIn was the most informative sub: modal for database products, side-by-side for issue trackers, new page for CRMs.

Two codebook faults account for most of this packet. (1) columnSummary puts None inside a pick-any, so 'no summary' can be written ['None'] or [], and that alone is the Trello and Basecamp disagreements — None should be the empty array. (2) columns cannot say whether to code the board as configured or the product's capability: Linear, ClickUp and Planner all ship grouped by status with a group-by-anything control, and the two readings give different variations. Smaller: transitions mixes enforcement (Allowed transitions only, Required fields) with side effects (Automation on move), and since nearly every product in this sample can fire a rule on a move, Automation on move stops discriminating; and Quick filters, Saved views and Sonnet's +Custom filter builder overlap badly — Pipedrive's saved-filter dropdown is defensibly any of the three.
sonnet: cardFields and filters are coded from general product capability rather than only what a single screenshot would show, per the protocol; swimlane basis for Azure DevOps (11) is a best guess, not a confident recall.

Three patterns stood out. (1) cardFields has no way to represent a monetary value that is the point of a sales-pipeline card (Pipedrive, HubSpot deals, Salesforce Opportunities all needed +Amount or value) — I had been forcing this into 'Estimate,' which is specifically an effort/points field and reads wrong for a dollar figure. (2) 'openIn' for the same product can differ by screen type within one product (Salesforce's Kanban card opens New page even though the codebook's own Side-by-side exemplar is Salesforce's list-view split view) — the codebook's per-product examples risk being read as per-product defaults when they are really per-screen. (3) Several CRM/PM tools (HubSpot, ClickUp, Airtable, monday.com) converge on the same four-part filter bar (a keyword search, an assignee-me toggle, one-click presets, and named saved configurations), and getting the boundary between 'Quick filters' and 'Only my items' right depended on whether a rater's note named a concrete mechanism or just asserted the value — worth flagging that this sub-dimension rewards specific product recall much more than most others in this entry.

recorded.name: Dedicated wizard flow
recorded.gloss: The bulk action runs through a separate multi-step wizard page (choose items, choose operation, confirm), not an inline toolbar, floating bar or menu, e.g. Jira's Bulk Change

fable: Surface as pick-one strains when a product offers both a context menu and a drop target (Finder, Explorer); I coded the one the sample's flow names.

Three variations were proposed by all three raters under different names (the wizard page, the gather-while-dragging selection, the keyboard-only surface), so they are missing values. surface as pick one strains wherever two surfaces coexist (Finder, Dropbox). A phone's swapped bottom toolbar is neither 'replaces the header' nor a floating bar. Preview of affected items and Confirm first overlap. execution depends on set size for Shopify, HubSpot and Mailchimp.
opus: surface needed three proposals, which says the sub assumes the action lives on the collection screen; a wizard page, a command palette and a bare keyboard shortcut are all common and none is expressible. consequence is pick-one but products stack them — Gmail confirms nothing and offers undo, AWS previews and confirms, Photos confirms with a recoverable trash — so I coded the strongest guard the flow puts in the way. execution is hard to observe: whether a bulk edit runs inline or as a job usually only shows at large N, and I coded the product's behaviour at scale.

The clearest finding here is not a fault but a fact about proposals: three raters found the same four gaps (a wizard surface, a side-panel surface, a keyboard-only surface, and a touch pick-up-and-gather selection) and named each of them differently, so the packet reports disagreement where there is none. The codebook faults proper: `surface` is pick one but Finder, Dropbox and Linear each show two surfaces at once, and worse, the codebook glosses two different surface variations with the same Finder instance (Context menu 'e.g., Finder' and Drop onto a target 'e.g., Drag to trash'). `consequence` mixes exclusive and non-exclusive values — Count only means 'the count and nothing more', so it cannot be tied against Confirm first or Undo afterwards the way the other variations can, and Spotify shows neither a count nor an undo. `selection`'s variations are named by desktop input (Shift-click range, Marquee), leaving every touch range gesture homeless. And `execution` is not a property of the design at all: the same Shopify or Mailchimp flow is immediate for three items and a background job for thirty thousand, so without a stated selection size raters will keep splitting.
sonnet: Several bulk-action surfaces (a dedicated wizard, a persistent side panel, keyboard-only application) don't fit the four listed surface variations, all of which assume some visible toolbar/menu/bar; consequence for AWS terminate (17) genuinely has both a preview and a confirmation, coded as Confirm first since the action is irreversible.

Two patterns stood out. (1) 'surface' converged on three separate new variations (Wizard, Command palette, Keyboard shortcut) across only 18 instances — this pick-one dimension's four enumerated values (Contextual toolbar, Floating action bar, Context menu, Drop onto a target) all assume the action surface appears ON the collection screen, which misses an entire family of patterns where the action is invoked elsewhere (a separate wizard page, a typed command, or no surface at all). (2) A touch-drag gesture that selects a contiguous run (Apple Photos, Apple Mail) is functionally the same selection outcome as Shift-click range even though the input mechanics differ (finger-drag vs click-shift-click) — I initially proposed a new value for this before recognizing both other raters treat it as the same existing concept, which I now think is the better reading of what the dimension is actually asking.

fable: Container style has no variation for the borderless card that most consumer grids use; nine of twenty needed +Flat. Style for bordered-vs-shadowed cards (Zillow, Amazon) is a fine visual distinction hard to recall exactly.

style has no value for the borderless card that most consumer grids use, and all three raters proposed one. Outlined versus Borderless is a one-pixel detail hard to recall for Amazon and Zillow. target has no value for a card whose several links all open one place while the card body is inert (Booking), and Separate targets is read differently when a nested link goes elsewhere (YouTube).
opus: style is the one real gap and it is a big one: half the sample uses no container at all, which Material's elevated/filled/outlined triad cannot say. shape reads as a layout question but its variations mix stacking direction (Vertical, Horizontal) with size (Compact tile); I used Compact tile only for Netflix's bare art tile. actions is pick-one and hover-only actions made it awkward — I counted an action that appears on hover (Pinterest's Save, Netflix's row) because it is on the card, and did not count context menus or edit affordances. target's Separate targets per attribute never applied cleanly: several cards have a nested secondary link (YouTube's channel, Amazon's ratings) without that being a design choice about where the item opens.

Most of this packet is one codebook fault: `style` borrows Material's elevated/filled/outlined triad, which has no value for the containerless card that half the sample uses (all three of us proposed one, two of us by the same name) and no rule for a card that is both filled and outlined (Linear, Apple News, Zillow) — it should be pick any, or its variations should be ordered as cues to read at rest. Second: `target` has no value for 'the content region but not the container', which is what YouTube, Amazon and Booking actually do, and its Separate targets per attribute gloss conflates several distinct targets with several distinct destinations. Third: `shape` mixes stacking direction with size, so a small vertical card (Google Play) has two defensible codes.
sonnet: style is the sub-dimension the Material-3-derived vocabulary (Elevated/Filled/Outlined) fits worst: most real browse/shopping/media tiles in this sample are borderless flat tiles rather than any of the three, hence the +Borderless proposal covering well over half the instances.

One dominant pattern: 'style' has no value for the no-container-at-all look that most modern consumer overview cards actually use (Airbnb, Amazon, Etsy, Pinterest, Netflix, Uber Eats, Facebook Marketplace, Spotify, YouTube, Google Play) — all three raters independently proposed essentially the same missing variation (my and opus's names matched exactly as 'Borderless,' fable's 'Flat' names the same thing), which is as strong a convergence signal as this reconciliation produced anywhere; the three existing values (Elevated/Filled/Outlined) assume every card has some kind of visible container, which turned out to be the minority case in this sample. A second, smaller pattern: 'target' undercounts cards where multiple elements link to genuinely different destinations (Amazon: image/title to the product, stars to reviews) versus cards where multiple clickable elements all lead to the same place (Booking.com) — the latter isn't really 'separate targets per attribute' the way the gloss's own example implies, and I initially conflated the two.

fable: Grab lacks the commonest desktop case, a plain drag from anywhere on the item; twelve of twenty needed +Drag anywhere. Indication (line vs gap vs reflow) is a fine detail of motion that I could not always recall with certainty (YouTube, VS Code).

grab lacks the plain pointer drag, which all three raters proposed. Into nesting and Onto a target to act overlap for dropping into a folder, and the codebook's own examples put folders under the latter. indication is a motion detail that cannot be settled from product memory.
opus: grab's Long-press anywhere is written as a touch idiom, so twelve desktop instances that simply drag the item had nowhere to go — that is the entry's one real gap. Keyboard lift and move was coded nowhere: accessible drag-and-drop exists in some of these products but is invisible unless you go looking, which makes the variation unobservable rather than absent. indication's Live reflow versus Placeholder gap is a genuinely fine call on a board — I used Placeholder gap only where a single empty slot opens and Live reflow where every neighbour moves. Into nesting is doing double duty for outline indentation and for dropping into a container; edge is n/a for fixed-size strips like the Dock and the taskbar.

Twelve of the twenty-six cells in this packet are the same missing variation, and all three of us proposed it independently under three names — `grab` has no value for a plain pointer press-and-drag, because Long-press anywhere is written as a touch idiom. Second fault: `destinations` and `edge` overlap, so a behaviour that happens at the edge of a container (tearing a tab off into a new window) can be coded as either, and `edge` assumes every container can be longer than the screen — a fixed strip that shrinks to fit (Chrome tabs, the Dock, the taskbar) has no answer but n/a. Third: Into nesting and Onto a target to act both describe dropping onto another item, separated only by whether the result is containment or an action, which splits the home screens and Finder three ways. The remaining cells are not codebook problems at all: they are memory disputes about what a specific product draws while dragging (YouTube's playlist), which no amount of reconciliation settles.
sonnet: grab is the sub-dimension the four variations fit worst for desktop pointer UIs: most of this sample's mouse-drag cases (12 of 20) have no dedicated handle and aren't a touch long-press either, hence the large +Click anywhere proposal.

One dominant pattern, one retraction. (1) 'grab' has no value for the desktop-pointer default — press the item itself and move, no handle, no hold delay — which is how the large majority of desktop drag-reorder surfaces in this sample actually work (Trello, Spotify, Chrome, the Dock, Finder, Keep, Figma, Slides, PowerPoint, Jira, VS Code, the Taskbar); all three raters independently proposed essentially the same missing value, and fable's and opus's names matched exactly ('Drag anywhere'), which I'm adopting over my own near-identical 'Click anywhere.' (2) I initially proposed a new 'edge' value ('Detach on drop off') for tab tear-off into a new window, but on reconsideration this doesn't actually answer the edge sub-dimension's own question (what happens when the destination is off-screen) — it's a different phenomenon, already reasonably captured by 'destinations: Across lists,' and both other raters' specific, corroborated claims that the tab strip itself auto-scrolls when crowded is the real, on-topic answer I'd missed by conflating two separate behaviours.

recorded.name: Flat AND/OR chain
recorded.gloss: A single ordered list of conditions joined throughout by one chosen AND or OR operator, more flexible than per-attribute facets (AND across, OR within) but without the nested groups of a full boolean builder, e.g. Airtable's classic view filter

fable: Logic as pick-one loses information where a product ANDs by default but also supports negation or a boolean mode (Gmail, GitHub, Jira); I coded the surface's primary behaviour and noted the rest.

Per query and In the URL overlap on every retail site. logic as pick one loses the AND-by-default surface whose query language also negates (Gmail, GitHub) or has a boolean mode (Jira). Preset brackets for price and date are read as Range or Date range by some raters and as values by others. Counts per value and Live results co-occur on facet rails.
opus: logic is effectively a constant: sixteen of twenty are AND across, OR within, because that is what a facet rail means, and the other four are database query builders. The sub would say more if it separated 'can values be excluded' from 'how do filters combine'. origin's Any attribute only fires for products where the data is the user's own (spreadsheets, databases, JQL); Natural language went unused in this sample, which is the honest finding — no shipping filter rail in the frame takes a sentence. preview and placement interact strongly: a rail filters live, a sheet commits with a count, and the one thing that breaks the pattern is LinkedIn committing from a dropdown. I coded the desktop behaviour where a product's mobile width adds an Apply button.

Fourteen of these forty-one cells are one codebook fault: `persistence` mixes durability with mechanism, and glosses two of its three variations with the same instances — Per query is 'e.g., Retail search' and In the URL is 'e.g., Most e-commerce', which are the same twelve sites. I code In the URL whenever the state is in the address and can be reloaded or shared, keeping Per query for the phone instances (Yelp, Google Maps) where there is no address to put it in; that partition is coherent but the codebook does not state it. Second fault: `types` mixes the widget with the predicate, so a preset relative date choice (LinkedIn's Date posted), a tier of price checkboxes (Nike) and a slider (Airbnb) are all arguably Range or Date range — and because `placement` names a chip bar, a chip that merely opens a panel gets coded as a Toggle chip type (I made that error on Google Flights). Third: `preview` is pick one but Booking.com genuinely shows counts per value *and* reloads live, and its None gloss ('Apply-then-see forms') reads as 'no feedback at all', which tempts a rater into coding None for a live-filtering page. Smaller: `logic`'s Exclusions is not on the same axis as the other two — negation can be added to either AND-across-OR-within facets or a boolean builder.
sonnet: preview mixes a live/default surface with a separate apply-gated panel in several products (Zillow, Yelp, LinkedIn); coded for the dominant/primary surface with the exception noted per instance, since preview is pick-one.

One dominant pattern: I systematically under-coded 'persistence' as the generic 'Per query' across roughly a dozen instances (Amazon, Airbnb, Google Shopping, Zillow, Booking.com, eBay, Google Flights, Etsy, LinkedIn, Indeed, Nike, Kayak) where both other raters specifically identified a URL parameter or fragment encoding the filter state — 'In the URL' should probably be treated as the default assumption for any web results page unless there's specific evidence otherwise, since it's cheap to implement and extremely common; 'Per query' should be reserved for cases with actual evidence the state resets and isn't shareable. A second, smaller pattern: 'preview' has three closely related values (Counts per value, Live results, Count on the apply button) that can all plausibly describe the same screen depending on which mechanism you emphasize (Booking.com and LinkedIn both genuinely have two of these at once) — the codebook could use a rule for which one wins when several apply, the way it does for arrangement's Zillow list-plus-map case elsewhere in this study.

fable: Multi-selection behaviour is unobservable from product knowledge for several tools (coded ? on four). Apply is Live for every instance, so it does not discriminate in this sample.

All properties and Contextual to the selection type overlap because every inspector follows the selection's type; the codebook should define All properties as exhaustive. apply wants pick any since Figma is live and scrubbable. The Floating palette example is dated for Adobe's docked panels. multi is unobservable from product memory for several tools.
opus: This entry is the most uniform in my slice: right sidebar, collapsible sections, live apply is the answer 14 times out of 20, which is itself the finding — the inspector has converged. set conflates two things and I applied a rule to stay consistent: a property search field makes it Searchable, even where All properties would also be true (Unreal, Android Studio, Godot). apply's Live and Scrub to preview are not alternatives — scrubbing is live editing with a drag gesture — so Figma is the only instance where I chose the more specific value, and a rater who reads apply as 'when does the edit commit' would code it Live. Pinned favourites went unused.

Three codebook faults account for nearly all of this packet. `grouping` offers Flat, Collapsible sections and Tabs but has no value for fixed, non-folding named sections, which is what Xcode, Sketch and Illustrator actually have — so the same panel is coded Flat by a rater reading 'do they collapse?' and Collapsible by one reading 'is it sectioned?'. `placement` mixes where the panel sits with what kind of window it is: Adobe's dockable palettes sit in a right column by default, so Floating palette and Right sidebar are both literally true, and the list has no left side at all (all three of us hit Canva). `multi` was a third of the packet and almost none of it is a reading of the product: multi-selection behaviour is rarely visible in a screen note, so it is coded from knowledge of the tool, and a rater who codes only what the note states will say Single object only every time — the sub-dimension needs an explicit 'not observable on this screen' instruction. Smaller: `set` mixes the contents (All / Contextual) with the access mechanism (Searchable, Pinned), so a searchable inspector always has two true codes, and `apply` has the same problem with Live plus Scrub to preview.
sonnet: placement for IDE/engine inspectors that default to a lower-right dock (Blender) is approximated as Bottom panel per the codebook's own game-engine-inspector gloss, even outside a literal game engine.

One dominant pattern: I systematically under-coded 'multi' as 'Single object only' across roughly half this archetype's instances (Xcode, Framer, Sketch, Keynote, PowerPoint, Godot) where both other raters specifically named a concrete 'Mixed'/'shared properties' UI element for multi-selection — every one of these tools does support it, and 'Single object only' should probably be my default assumption only when a rater specifically denies multi-selection support, not whenever I simply don't recall seeing it demonstrated. A smaller pattern: 'placement' assumes an inspector opposite the canvas is always a right sidebar, which Canva's left-docked panel (and both other raters' identically-named proposal for it) shows isn't universal.

fable: Persistence lacks the commonest case, a single remembered layout for the app (nine of twenty). Create is n/a for fixed layouts where the user never makes a split.

persistence lacks the commonest case, one layout remembered for the app, which two raters proposed. create needs [] rather than n/a for fixed layouts. sizing wants pick any where a fixed layout also collapses a pane or a snap layout also drags. Grid of panes and Nested splits are undefined for dock systems.
opus: This entry's unit ('one window layout') stretches over two different things: layouts a person builds (VS Code, tmux, Snap) and fixed multi-region app chromes (Mail, Slack, Discord, Figma). For the latter, create is empty and the interesting sub-dimensions are relationship and sizing. persistence needed the one proposal: eight instances remember the layout forever as an app setting, which is neither per session, a saved layout nor per workspace. sizing is pick-one but collapsible and draggable coexist almost everywhere, so I coded the seam behaviour and treated collapse as secondary. Nothing in the entry can express the responsive reflow that DevTools and many web layouts do when the window narrows.

Two thirds of this packet is one missing variation in `persistence`: eight of the twenty instances simply remember their layout for the application, which is neither Per session, Saved layouts nor Per workspace — fable and I proposed it independently (I have taken fable's name, +App-wide) and sonnet, having no value for it, coded Per session eight times. The rest divides into three smaller faults. `create` is pick any but has no way to say 'nobody creates this split, it is the app's own layout', so six instances are coded as an empty list by two raters and n/a by the third, which scores as disagreement; it also names its variations after editor idioms (a *tab* dragged to an edge), which forces a judgement call for window tiling. `orientation`'s Grid of panes and Nested splits are not exclusive — every dock system that nests arbitrarily also renders as a grid, so Photoshop, JupyterLab and Discord split us. And `sizing` lists only pointer mechanisms, so a keyboard-resized layout (tmux) has no value.
sonnet: create is left empty for several fixed, built-in split layouts (Mail's three columns, Slack's thread pane, Gmail's reading pane) where the split isn't made through a menu command, tab drag or keyboard shortcut the way an IDE split is, but is a toggled built-in feature instead.

Two patterns stood out. (1) 'persistence' has no value for the single most common case in this sample: a layout simply remembered for the whole app across restarts, with no session boundary, no named-layout picker and no per-project scoping (Apple Mail, Outlook, Slack, Discord, GitHub, Figma, DevTools, Gmail) — I'd been defaulting to 'Per session' for lack of a better fit, but both other raters independently converged on essentially the same missing value, which is as strong a signal as this reconciliation produced anywhere. (2) 'create' needed a genuine n/a (not an empty array) for fixed, built-in multi-pane layouts that no user action constructs (Apple Mail, Slack's thread pane, Discord, Figma, DevTools, Beyond Compare) — these aren't cases where the three create mechanisms were checked and found absent, but cases where the concept of 'making a split' doesn't apply to a layout the app always provides.

fable: Conflicts for cell-based tools were coded Last-write wins at the cell, since only same-cell edits ever conflict; OT/CRDT was reserved for character- or object-level merging.

conflicts: the four values mix mechanism, policy and prevention and say nothing about merge granularity — since the OT/CRDT exemplar Figma is itself last-writer-per-property, I now read that value as 'automatic silent merge at the product's edit unit' and reserve Last-write wins for whole-artifact replacement; the Locked regions exemplar 'Cell locks in Sheets' is a permission feature, not conflict handling. presence: 'Async activity only' is named as exclusive inside a pick-any sub. access: Notion/Confluence/GitHub each truthfully hold two values; wants pick-any.
opus: access is pick-one over products that run two schemes at once: GitHub has both roles and branches, Notion both roles and page-level locks, Sheets both roles and protected ranges. It also has no variation for access that follows from membership of a container — a Slack canvas is readable because you are in the channel, not because anyone shared it. presence conflates being here with having been here, which is why Apple Notes and Trello, both live, came out looking async.

presence mixes an exclusive negative with a positive: 'Async activity only' says there is no live channel, so it reads as contradicting 'Named authorship on edits' even though every async product in this sample names its authors — that one word drove four of the thirteen presence splits. access stays pick-one over products that run two schemes at once (GitHub roles plus branches, Confluence space groups plus page restrictions) and should be pick any; and the Locked regions exemplar 'Cell locks in Sheets' is a standing permission, not a concurrency strategy, which pulled two raters onto it.
sonnet: Presence was a frequent judgment call between Live cursors and avatars and Named authorship on edits for tools that show real-time updates and avatars but not a literal moving text cursor (Notes, Trello, GitHub) — I reserved Live cursors and avatars for products I'm confident render an actual cursor/selection indicator, and used Named authorship where the cue is really attribution after the fact.

Two codebook-shaped findings: (1) presence's 'Async activity only' reads as if it excludes the other values, but it routinely co-occurs with Named authorship on edits (GitHub, Apple Notes, SharePoint check-out) since the two describe different axes — temporal mode versus attribution richness — not alternatives; (2) my round-1 '+Inherited from a container's membership' access proposal (Slack Canvas, Google Drive folder) was unnecessary — it's Role-based permissions applied at a container that cascades, which the sharing-permissions archetype's scope dimension (Folder and children) already covers; access in this archetype does not need a fifth value for it.

lifecycle assumes every annotation is a social thread someone closes — Kindle, Pages, Hypothesis and Loom have no close state and all came out n/a — and its first two values are not exclusive: Docs, the exemplar for Open until resolved, also keeps resolved threads in a history, which is what split Miro and Canva. layout is pick-one over products that have both an in-situ thread and an aggregate list (Kindle's Notebook, Pages' Comments pane, Acrobat's list), and its Review page list gloss names GitHub Files changed, a screen where the thread is literally inline under the block, so two values name one screen. marker has no value for the commonest code-review case, where the thread in place is the only mark.

usage: People follow a lead designer during critiques instead of screensharing
questions: When does showing idle location become uncomfortable monitoring?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Sidebar people list: VS Code Live Share — Shared session

Summon or call in-file: VS Code Live Share — Shared session

Show everyone: VS Code Live Share — Shared session

fable: Density is Collapse to count almost everywhere because every avatar stack overflows to +N; lifecycle beyond While connected is only visible in Google's idle greying.

density cannot be coded from memory of a normal session — Show everyone vs Collapse to count depends on an overflow threshold nobody sees, so one rater defaulted to each; the codebook should say what to code when the crowded case is unobserved. placement: the Sidebar people list exemplar (Notion) is a top stack, and there is no value for a list behind a button (Pages). scope: file-wide avatars with per-page cursors (Figma, FigJam, Slides) fit neither This file nor This page or frame cleanly.
opus: density is close to unobservable: how a product behaves with forty people in a file is something almost nobody sees, so those codes are inferences from the avatar stack's design rather than observations. Hide my cursor also went unused — no instance in this sample offers a privacy toggle, which is itself worth reporting. scope is pick-one but a session-based tool (Live Share) has presence that follows people across files, which none of the variations describes.

density stayed the hardest sub-dimension to apply honestly — nobody watches a file with forty people in it, so most density codes are inferences from how the avatar stack is built, and I moved two to ? rather than keep inferring. scope is pick one but wants pick any: a board with pages (FigJam) is scoped both to the file and to the page, and Live Share's presence follows a person across files, which no variation says. cues has no slot for expressive, momentary cues (cursor chat, stamps), hence the adopted proposal, and placement's Sidebar people list has to absorb popover lists (Pages) that are not sidebars.
sonnet: Density came back Show everyone for almost every instance since none of these sample screens describe a crowded session; Collapse to count only showed up where the note explicitly mentions a count (Docs, Coda), so this dimension is likely undercounted relative to what these products actually do at higher participant counts, which I have no direct evidence of in the sample.

My own round-1 density codes had a systematic bias: I answered 'Show everyone' as a small-team default across nearly the whole sample instead of checking each product's own overflow behaviour, when most mainstream tools here (Figma, the Workspace and Office families, Canva, Airtable, Slides, Linear, Whiteboard) are well known to collapse a crowded avatar stack to a '+N' count; I've corrected those and held Show everyone only where a rater gave a specific small-scale reason (Replit, tldraw, Pages, Overleaf). Separately, cues is pick-any but I was treating Avatar and colour and Named cursor as if picking one excluded the other, undercounting Avatar and colour across most of the entry even where the sample note names avatars directly.
