entries.name: Sharing and permissions
entries.definition: Granting, reviewing and revoking who can view, comment on or edit a shared artifact, and how they receive access.

dimensions.name: Permission model
dimensions.question: What rights can be granted?

dimensions.name: Share invocation
dimensions.question: How is sharing started?

dimensions.name: Permission scope
dimensions.question: What does a grant apply to?

dimensions.name: Sharing feedback
dimensions.question: How does the person know who has access and what changed?

dimensions.name: Grant lifecycle
dimensions.question: How do grants start, change and end?

dimensions.name: Policy initiative
dimensions.question: Who decides the default sharing posture?

wild.note: Link access and role menus are routinely changed; inheritance and expiry less often.

techniques.name: Access as a visible list
techniques.how: Always show principals and roles as an editable collection, including link principals, not only a success toast.

techniques.name: Warn before widening
techniques.how: When a change expands audience (especially external), show who newly gains access before confirming.

techniques.name: Suggest least privilege
techniques.how: Recommend the narrowest role that matches the stated intent (“collect feedback” → commenter).

entries.sample: Cloud drives, design libraries, code hosts and enterprise content platforms.
entries.unit: One share configuration for one artifact or container.
usage: People copy links before setting the role, then fix oversharing later
questions: How should inherited permissions be explained without a full directory tree?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Lifecycle is Until revoked nearly everywhere; expiring links are options rather than the default. Branch protection is a policy, not a share flow, so openBy is n/a.

lifecycle and initiative are pick-one but nearly every product truthfully holds a default (until revoked; person chooses) plus an option (expiry; org default) — both want pick-any. scope's Time-limited access duplicates lifecycle's Expiring access. Sonnet's lists omit Anonymous link access wherever a link exists, which reads roles as a person-role ladder only; the gloss should say whether a link audience is a role.
opus: scope puts Time-limited access beside Whole file and Folder and children, which are answers to a different question; I coded expiry under lifecycle throughout and left that variation unused, which I think is where the codebook is wrong rather than where the products are. The entry also has no way to record a principal that is a group or a room (a Slack channel, a GitHub team) rather than a person or a link, and roles cannot say that commenting comes bundled with viewing rather than as its own grade (Figma).

lifecycle is pick one but several products hold two values at once — a grant that lasts until revoked plus an optional expiry on the link (Dropbox, OneDrive, Box) — so I applied the codebook's own ordering and coded Until revoked; it wants to be pick any. scope still carries Time-limited access, which answers the lifecycle question rather than the scope one, and that mis-parking is what split us on OneDrive. roles has no way to say that a right is bundled rather than granted (Figma's commenting rides with viewing) and no principal type for a group or a room (a Slack channel, a GitHub team), and openBy has no value for a screen where nothing is shared at all (branch protection) short of n/a.
sonnet: None of these 20 instances showed AI-suggested recipients ('people you worked with') as the primary mechanism, so that Initiative variation went unused rather than being force-applied to ordinary invite-by-email flows that may also have it as a secondary autocomplete feature I'm not confident about per-product.

Two codebook overlaps and one convention question: (1) scope's Time-limited access and lifecycle's Expiring access share the same exemplar (an expiring link) — the same real feature can be legitimately coded under either or, as I initially did, double-coded under both; I settled on scope answering what the grant covers and lifecycle answering how it ends. (2) openBy's From a parent folder policy is ambiguous between an item's access having arrived FROM an ancestor's policy and an item being the SOURCE whose children inherit downstream — two raters credited a folder/page's own share screen with this value on downstream-inheritance evidence, which I don't think the value is describing. (3) roles' Custom fine-grained: whether it stacks additively with the simpler named roles it subsumes (GitHub's ladder ticked as View/Edit/Owner too) or stands alone as the codebook's own GitHub exemplar suggests — I read it as standing alone.

entries.name: Version history
entries.definition: A browsable record of past states of an artifact, with authorship, so a person can compare, restore or branch from an earlier version.

dimensions.name: What a version captures
dimensions.question: What is stored and shown for each version?

values.name: Field change log
values.description: Each version is one field's old and new value rather than a document state (Airtable record revisions)

values.name: Field-level change log
values.description: A record of individual field-by-field changes (old value to new value, who and when), rather than a snapshot of the whole document, a named checkpoint, a commit, an autosave generation, or a branch tip.

dimensions.name: History layout
dimensions.question: How is the history presented?

values.name: Receding stack in 3D space
values.description: Past states are shown as a stack of documents/windows receding visually into the distance, navigated by a timeline, rather than a flat chronological list, a calendar grouping, a filmstrip of thumbnails, a commit graph, or a diff view.

dimensions.name: Comparing versions
dimensions.question: How do versions relate when inspected?

dimensions.name: Restore flow
dimensions.question: How does a person return to or reuse a past state?

dimensions.name: Opening history
dimensions.question: How is history entered and left?

dimensions.name: History feedback
dimensions.question: How does the person know what will happen on restore?

wild.note: Naming versions and filtering by author are common; diff granularity less so.

examples.name: Google Docs
examples.note: Name current version; browse by person

techniques.name: Named checkpoints
techniques.how: Let people pin meaningful versions with titles so the timeline is a story, not only autosaves.

techniques.name: Summarize this span
techniques.how: Generate a readable summary of changes between two versions, linked to the underlying diff.

techniques.name: Restore as a branch
techniques.how: Default restore creates a branch or named copy so the current tip is never silently destroyed.

entries.sample: Documents, design files, wikis and source control UIs.
entries.unit: One history timeline for one artifact.
usage: People name versions before big reviews so restore targets are obvious
questions: How fine should diffs be when the artifact is a canvas rather than text?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

recorded.name: Per-field change events
recorded.gloss: The timeline records individual changes — this field went from A to B, by whom, when — rather than states of the whole artifact; there is nothing to restore because there is no version

fable: Time Machine and Pages' versions browser are neither list nor filmstrip exactly; coded Filmstrip. git log is a command with no compare, restore or entry point of its own.

layout's Filmstrip exemplar (Figma) is a list without thumbnails; Canva is the real filmstrip. compare is pick-one but every git UI offers inline and split — the codebook should name a default rule. feedback's Author and timestamp conjoins two things personal histories only half have. Three raters proposed the same field-change-log capture under three names.
opus: layout and compare pull apart badly: a history that shows commits in a list and a diff in a pane is one layout or two depending on how you read it, and Side-by-side compare sits in layout while the diff variations sit in compare. Branch from here and Cherry-pick a change went unused even though four git instances support both, because pick-one made me take the restore each product leads with. Warning that restore is undoable also never appeared — none of these twenty warns before restoring.

Author and timestamp bundles two signals into one value, so a personal backup that is nothing but dated snapshots (Time Machine, Windows, Pages) cannot be coded truthfully either way — that bundling drove most of the feedback splits. layout cites Google Docs version history under both Chronological list and Calendar of days, so one screen satisfies two values; compare's Split diff cites GitHub, which actually opens a unified diff by default, and that wrong exemplar split all four git clients; and openBy mixes entry routes with destination surfaces and has no value for a typed command.
sonnet: GitLab's repository-graph screen (14) and the raw git log --graph command (18) are both read-only overview views that don't themselves expose compare/restore actions (those live on other screens of the same product) — I coded those honestly as '?' or n/a rather than importing behaviour from a screen not actually sampled.

Three findings: (1) capture's values aren't mutually exclusive the way I treated them in round 1 — a named checkpoint or an autosave generation is still also a Full document snapshot, and I'd been picking only the more 'interesting' value instead of all that apply, which accounts for most of my changes here. (2) compare's Split diff vs Inline diff split across the git-family instances (GitHub, GitHub Desktop, Sourcetree, GitLab, VS Code) is a real, verifiable platform default in each case, not a matter of taste, but the codebook's 'pick one' doesn't flag that several of these tools offer both as a user toggle. (3) All three raters independently proposed near-identical new capture values for Airtable's field-level change log (my Field-level change log, fable's Field change log, opus's Per-field change events) — strong, convergent evidence this is a real gap regardless of which name is adopted.

entries.name: Communicate
entries.definition: Exchange messages with people over time, from a live call to an email answered next week.

dimensions.name: Conversation structure
dimensions.question: How are exchanges divided?

values.name: Proximity
values.description: Exchanges are divided by location in a shared space: you talk to whoever is near your avatar, plus room-wide and everyone channels

values.name: Proximity-based rooms
values.description: Exchanges are not persistent named streams but form dynamically among people whose avatars are spatially near each other on a shared map

dimensions.name: Tempo
dimensions.question: How synchronous is it, and does it last?

dimensions.name: Arrangement
dimensions.question: How are conversations and messages arranged?

values.name: Beside content
values.description: A single conversation runs in a column alongside the primary content (a live video), with no list of other conversations

values.name: Chat beside content
values.description: A single persistent chat column runs beside a media stage (a live stream, a visit) rather than beside a navigable list of separate conversations

dimensions.name: Assistance
dimensions.question: What does the system write or summarize?

dimensions.name: Audience
dimensions.question: How many people is it for?

dimensions.name: Signals
dimensions.question: What does the system say about delivery and presence?

wild.note: Notification rules, mute, read receipts and sidebar organization are often exposed.

techniques.name: Attention recipes
techniques.how: Per conversation, decide what reaches you, when, and in what form (interrupt, badge, digest), as an editable rule.

techniques.name: Thread ↔ channel morph
techniques.how: Promote a thread to its own channel, or fold a quiet channel into a thread, without losing history.

techniques.name: Catch me up
techniques.how: A summary of what changed, every line linked to the message it came from.

recorded.name: Docked beside content
recorded.gloss: A single conversation column pinned beside non-conversation content (a live video, a page), with no list of other conversations to move between

fable: audience is pick-one but nearly every product spans one-to-one, group and broadcast; coded the screen the sample locates. Structure/arrangement exemplars cite Slack and Gmail for two variations each, so I coded the default state (channel + sidebar; thread replaces list but label list stays). Assistance: 'None' used explicitly where the codebook lists it.

audience is pick one but messengers hold One-to-one, Small group and Broadcast at once (Telegram, WeChat, Messenger, Teams); it wants pick any. tempo's Near-synchronous gloss (Chat) names a medium, so live-only chat rooms split raters.
opus: audience is the weakest code here: every product supports one-to-one, groups and communities, so I took the audience the sampled screen centres and noted the rest. arrangement forced a choice between the resting layout and the panel-open layout for Slack-likes; I coded the resting layout consistently.

audience is the codebook's weak spot here: every product supports one-to-one, group and community audiences at once, so the sub-dimension wants to be pick any; structure names Slack for both Channels and Threads inside channels, which is why n=3 split three ways.
sonnet: Audience was hard to pin to one value for products whose sample screen names both a 1:1 and a group context (Telegram, Messenger, WeChat) — marked '?' rather than guess; noted in each _note.

Two codebook problems surfaced here. (1) `audience` is pick one but almost every messenger spans one-to-one, small group and broadcast in the same product — Telegram, WeChat and Messenger all forced raters into a dodge or a coin flip; it should be pick any, or its gloss should say 'the default audience of the screen's conversation'. (2) `structure`'s Channels and Threads inside channels are nested rather than exclusive and the codebook cites Slack for both, which is what split n=3; Threads inside channels should be glossed as implying channels, so the more specific code wins.

entries.name: Chat thread
entries.definition: A chronological sequence of messages between participants, with a composer at the edge.

dimensions.name: Message layout
dimensions.question: How are messages drawn?

dimensions.name: Reply structure
dimensions.question: How do replies relate to messages?

dimensions.name: Message content
dimensions.question: What can a message carry, and what metadata shows?

dimensions.name: Message lifetime
dimensions.question: What happens to a message over time?

dimensions.name: Composer actions
dimensions.question: What can be done from the composer?

dimensions.name: Unread position
dimensions.question: Where does a returning reader land?

wild.note: Density modes, themes and text size are common options.

techniques.name: Promote to structure
techniques.how: Turn any message into a task, a thread, a document or a pinned attribute in the header (a deadline found in chat, surfaced like CHI '25’s Response Deadline).

techniques.name: Density modes
techniques.how: Switch between bubbles, cozy and compact per conversation.

entries.sample: Consumer messaging, team chat and customer support chat.
usage: Decisions made in chat are lost because chat has no structure to keep them in
questions: Where is the overview of a conversation, and what are its attributes?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

recorded.name: Labelled stream
recorded.gloss: One left-aligned stream where each run of messages sits under the sender's coloured name label, with neither bubbles nor avatars

fable: unread: the Slack/Discord exemplars both scroll to a divider, so I coded 'New messages divider' when a line is drawn and 'First unread' when the view lands on it without a line (Zulip) or per the Discord exemplar. lifetime is pick-one, so opt-in disappearing (Signal, Instagram) and scheduled send (Telegram, Slack) are noted rather than coded.
opus: lifetime is pick-one but most products have two answers at once (edit/delete plus scheduled send, or edit/delete plus an optional disappearing timer). I ruled that lifetime describes a sent message's persistence — Disappearing only when the sampled screen's default or signature state is a timer, scheduled send only when nothing can be edited or deleted — and noted it per instance. The New messages divider / First unread split is also thin: I read divider as a marker you land above and First unread as the scroll position.
sonnet: Several messengers (Instagram, WeChat, LINE) support delete/unsend but not true message editing; coded them as 'Editable and deletable' since the codebook bundles both under one variation rather than splitting them.

entries.name: Comment thread
entries.definition: Discussion attached to an artifact or post, where replies nest and threads resolve.

dimensions.name: Nesting
dimensions.question: How do replies nest, and what are threads attached to?

values.name: Anchored threads
values.description: One thread per location in an artifact

dimensions.name: Ordering
dimensions.question: Who decides which comments come first?

values.name: Anchor order
values.description: Threads are listed in the order of their anchors in the artifact (page position, timecode), not by time or votes

values.name: By anchor position
values.description: Threads are ordered by where their anchors fall in the artifact — down the document, along the timeline, through the pages — not by time or votes

dimensions.name: Resolution
dimensions.question: Does a thread end?

values.name: Marked status
values.description: A thread can be marked completed/accepted/rejected but stays in view rather than being hidden

dimensions.name: Placement
dimensions.question: Where do threads appear?

values.name: Inline at the anchor
values.description: The thread is spliced into the artifact itself, pushing it apart — a review thread expanding under the diff line it annotates — rather than sitting in a margin or panel

values.name: Bottom sheet
values.description: Comments slide up as a sheet over the lower part of the screen while the content stays playing or visible above

values.name: Inline at anchor
values.description: The thread renders directly in the content flow at its anchored location (e.g., under a diff line) rather than offset to a margin column, a side panel, or as a pin on a canvas

dimensions.name: Long threads
dimensions.question: How are long threads condensed?

dimensions.name: Moderation
dimensions.question: How is the discussion kept healthy?

wild.note: Sort order is often a choice; structure is not.

examples.name: Reddit
examples.note: Sort comments by Best, Top, New, Controversial

techniques.name: Thread lenses
techniques.how: Collapse a discussion by participant, by resolved state or by stance, as lenses rather than filters that hide.

techniques.name: Summarize the disagreement
techniques.how: A summary of positions, each linked to the comments that hold it.

entries.sample: Social, news, code review, document and design collaboration tools.
entries.unit: One comment thread or thread set on one artifact.
usage: Most readers never go past the top few comments
questions: When comments are anchored, is the artifact the overview?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Anchored threads: Figma — Comments on a design file

Newest first: Figma — Comments on a design file
The New York Times — Article comments

Resolve and hide: Figma — Comments on a design file
Locked: The New York Times — Article comments

Side panel: The New York Times — Article comments
Pins on a canvas: Figma — Comments on a design file

Show all: Figma — Comments on a design file

None: Figma — Comments on a design file

recorded.name: Sheet over the content
recorded.gloss: Comments open in a bottom sheet that slides up over the post or video rather than below or beside it

fable: ordering's 'Top by votes' had to stretch to cover engagement/relevance ranking (Instagram, Facebook, X, TikTok, Medium) since no 'ranked by relevance' variation exists. 'Pinned by author' was never coded as the primary ordering because a pin is an exception to whatever sort is default.

Resolve and hide bundles two things, marking a thread settled and removing it from view; review tools mark without hiding. Voting under moderation is read two ways, as a ranking signal (hearts, claps) or as a burying tool; the gloss should say which.
opus: ordering has no variation for algorithmic relevance (Most relevant, Top comments, ranked replies); I coded those Top by votes because a visible like count feeds the rank, but that reads more into it than the label says. Anchored products needed the +By anchor position proposal because none of the four time/vote orderings describe reading down a document.

ordering is pick one but a news or social thread offers newest, top and curated orders side by side on the same screen; it wants to be pick any with a marked default. nesting has nothing between One level of replies and Reddit-deep.
sonnet: Ordering was often a fit-by-analogy: several products (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X) default to an undisclosed relevance/engagement algorithm that most resembles 'Top by votes' without being literal vote counts; two products (Medium, Substack) got '?' where I couldn't recall the exact default confidently.

Three codebook problems. (1) Moderation's Voting has no gloss on whether a one-directional like or clap counts as a vote; that single ambiguity produced six of this entry's nine moderation disagreements, and it should say so explicitly. (2) Resolve and hide bundles two separate things — marking a thread settled and removing it from view — which is why review tools (Frame.io, Acrobat) needed the Marked status proposal. (3) Placement's Pins on a canvas and Side panel are both true of most anchored tools at once (a marker on the artifact, the thread body in a panel); the gloss needs a rule — I coded where the thread body renders — or the sub should be pick any. Nesting also asks two questions at once (how deep replies go, and what the thread is attached to), so Anchored threads competes with a depth answer rather than excluding it.

entries.name: Inbox
entries.definition: A list of messages or requests awaiting attention, each opened, acted on and cleared.

dimensions.name: Organization
dimensions.question: How are messages sorted into places, and grouped?

dimensions.name: Reading arrangement
dimensions.question: Where does a message open, and how dense is the list?

dimensions.name: Triage model
dimensions.question: What does clearing a message mean?

values.name: Close or solve
values.description: Clearing means setting the ticket's status to solved/closed; assignment is a step along the way, not the clearing act

values.name: Reading is triage
values.description: Nothing is archived or filed: an item leaves the attention list simply by being read (HEY's Previously seen, Slack Activity)

values.name: Mark as read
values.description: Clearing means marking read: there is no destination, no archive and no file — the item simply stops being unread

dimensions.name: Row attributes
dimensions.question: What does each row show?

values.name: Assignee
values.description: The row shows who owns the item — an avatar or name for the teammate it is assigned to — which only exists in shared inboxes

values.name: Status
values.description: The row shows a workflow state the item moves through (new, open, pending, solved) and often a priority field, distinct from a user-applied label

dimensions.name: Prioritization
dimensions.question: Who decides what matters first?

dimensions.name: Deferral
dimensions.question: How can a message come back later?

wild.note: Email is one of the few overview–detail interfaces where layout and density are routinely offered.

examples.name: Gmail
examples.note: Reading pane position, density, inbox type, category tabs on or off

examples.name: Outlook
examples.note: Focused Inbox and conversation view toggles

techniques.name: Surfaced deadlines
techniques.how: Generate an attribute such as Response Deadline from message bodies, surface it into rows and sort by it (CHI '25 §5.1.3), generalized to any extracted field.

techniques.name: Rule from example
techniques.how: Select a few messages and file them; the inbox proposes the rule and the split it would create.

techniques.name: Split by query
techniques.how: Any saved search becomes its own inbox section, reorderable and collapsible.

entries.sample: Email clients, shared inboxes, support desks and notification triage tools.
usage: Zero-inbox people and pilers use the same product in opposite ways
questions: Should extracted attributes (deadlines, amounts) be treated as first-class email metadata?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

recorded.name: Sort into stacks
recorded.gloss: Clearing a message means dragging it into a designated pile (e.g., Set Aside, Reply Later) rather than filing, archiving, snoozing on a timer, or assigning it to someone

fable: organization is n/a for single-list notification inboxes (Linear, Notion). priority: 'Importance markers' used whenever rows carry an importance flag though sort stays chronological (Gmail, Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk). Gmail's Labels vs Automatic categories overlap: coded the storage model, not the default view.

organization mixes a storage model (Folders, Labels) with a view model (Automatic categories, Split inboxes), so Gmail and Apple Mail hold two values at once. Replace and New page both mean the list goes away and need a sharper line. density is Gmail-relative with no absolute anchor. Bundles overlaps Automatic categories.
opus: triage is pick-one but mail clients offer archive, file and snooze at once; I coded the product's primary clearing gesture and noted the rest. organization does not fit notification inboxes (Notion has no organising structure at all, coded n/a; GitHub's repo grouping and Slack's filter tabs I read as Automatic categories). rowAttributes had no way to say assignee or status, which is most of what a support row carries.

organization is pick one but Proton, Gmail and Apple Mail all run two systems at once (folders and labels, labels and automatic categories), so it wants to be pick any; and organization's Automatic categories overlaps grouping's Bundles for Spark and GitHub, which is where those two subs split us.
sonnet: Ticketing tools (Zendesk, Freshdesk) carry priority/status fields that only loosely map onto rowAttributes' vocabulary (built for email, not tickets); coded the closest available values rather than proposing a ticket-specific field.

Four codebook problems. (1) organization is pick one but Gmail is the codebook's own exemplar for both Labels and Automatic categories, and Proton and Apple Mail genuinely have two filing models at once — it should be pick any, or the gloss should say to code the storage model and let categories be a view. (2) organization and grouping overlap: bundling can be read as either, which is what split GitHub and Spark; I resolved it by a rule (organization = how the list is divided into places, grouping = what one row represents) and the codebook should state it. (3) density has no absolute anchor — its three values are Gmail's own settings, so for every product without a density control raters were judging spaciousness by feel, which produced six disagreements. (4) triage is missing two whole models that the sample kept hitting, status-close (helpdesks) and nothing-to-file (HEY, Slack), and rowAttributes, built for email, has no owner or workflow state; both adopted proposals came from that.

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Content beside speakers: FaceTime — Call on Apple Vision Pro

Automatic quality: Gather — Space with a video conversation

recorded.name: Avatars in a space
recorded.gloss: People are avatars in a shared virtual space rather than tiles; video exists only for whoever your avatar is standing near

fable: constraints is pick-one but most products offer automatic quality plus something more specific; I coded the most specific adaptation the product offers (dial-in, low-data, audio-only) and Automatic quality only when nothing more specific exists. attention and tile are partly unobservable from memory for the smaller products (Whereby, Messenger, Huddles) so some lists are conservative.

tile's Live captions exemplar (Meet) is a caption line along the bottom, not on a tile, so raters split on whether captions belong to the tile; say where. constraints is pick one but products hold dial-in, audio-only and low-data at once; it wants pick any or a most-specific rule.
opus: constraints is pick-one but nearly every product has several fallbacks, so I ranked them Dial-in > Low-data mode > Audio only > Automatic quality and coded the deepest one each product offers as an explicit affordance. tile's Live captions never fired: every product I know draws captions along the bottom of the stage, not on a person's tile — worth checking whether that variation describes anything real.

Two codebook faults drove most of this entry: Live captions sits under Tile information although captions are a call-level overlay in every product that has them, and constraints is pick one although automatic quality is glossed 'All' and stacks under dial-in, audio-only and low-data — it should be pick any, or automatic quality should be dropped as the baseline.
sonnet: attention is unobservable from general product knowledge for most non-flagship tools (only Zoom and Google Meet are cited by the codebook itself); coded '?' rather than guess for the majority of instances.

Three codebook problems, and this entry's low kappa comes almost entirely from them. (1) constraints is unusable as pick one because its first value, Automatic quality, is glossed 'e.g., All' — it is true of every instance, so a rater who codes it honestly records nothing and a rater who codes the distinctive adaptation records something else; it should be pick any, or Automatic quality should be dropped as a baseline. (2) withContent came out Content with filmstrip for all thirteen disputed cells, because the other two values (Content beside speakers, Presenter over slides) are opt-in modes of a single product rather than layouts a product chooses — the sub barely discriminates as written. (3) tile's Live captions is ambiguous about where the caption renders: most products draw captions at the bottom of the window with a speaker name rather than on the tile, which is why one rater coded it everywhere and another nowhere; I coded it wherever the call ships live captions and the codebook should say which it means. Minor: attention has no explicit 'None' value, so 'nothing applies' has to be an empty array.

values.description: Clicking (not hovering) a button reveals a picker of reaction options to choose from

questions: Should conventional reaction meanings be declared so they can drive views?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: add is pick-any of gestures, so a plain tap/click on an always-visible button (X, YouTube, Reddit, Medium, Zoom, Gmail) codes as an empty array; the codebook may want a 'Tap a button' variation. Slack is the exemplar for both Count per reaction and Who reacted; I coded the always-visible aggregate.

add has no value for the commonest case, a tap on a dedicated button; three raters proposed it under two names. aggregate assumes reactions persist and collect, transient call reactions do not fit. Total count vs Count per reaction needs to say whether glyphs beside one number count as per-reaction.
opus: add had no variation for the commonest case of all — a plain tap on a visible like button — so half the social instances needed +Single tap. aggregate is pick-one but Slack-likes show a count per reaction at rest and the names on hover, which are two different variations of the same system; I coded the resting display and noted the hover. Zoom's transient reactions have no aggregate at all, coded n/a.

aggregate has no value for what messaging apps actually draw — the distinct emoji glyphs with a single total beside them — so WhatsApp and Messenger split all three of us between Total count, Count per reaction and Who reacted.
sonnet: Vocabulary and aggregate were often close calls between two plausible codebook values for the same product (e.g., YouTube's visible like/hidden dislike split, Instagram's optional count-hiding); picked the value the codebook itself cites that product for where one exists.

Two codebook problems. (1) aggregate is pick one but its values are layers of the same display, not alternatives: WhatsApp and Messenger show a total at rest, per-reaction counts and who reacted on tap. It should be pick any, or the gloss should say to code what the resting surface shows — I coded the resting state. (2) add mixes two questions, what reveals the reaction control (hover, long-press, always visible) and what choosing looks like (one default reaction versus a picker); that is why one affordance drew three different codes and why both the Single tap and Click to open picker proposals were needed. Also worth noting: two raters independently proposed the same missing single-tap variation, so it is variation-worthy.

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

A device in the environment: Philips Hue app — Room light settings
Sonos app — Speaker settings and EQ
Appearance of the UI: Apple Watch app — Watch face editor

Flat list: Philips Hue app — Room light settings
Apple Watch app — Watch face editor

Immediate: Philips Hue app — Room light settings

Scheduled: iOS Focus — Set up a Focus

This account everywhere: iOS Focus — Set up a Focus

fable: Scope for home devices is awkward: the device in the environment is neither 'this device' (the phone) nor an account; I used This device to mean the target device and noted household sharing.

scope has no value for a device in the environment (Hue, thermostat, Sonos, Ring): This device reads as the client and One configured instance as a built product, so home-device scope splits raters. organization's Grouped sections (macOS System Settings) and Hierarchical panes (Apple Settings) examples are the same sidebar-and-pane design, so sidebar layouts split raters. application wants pick any: Notion mixes Save forms with instant toggles.
opus: organization has no variation for configuration by direct manipulation of a model rather than by a catalogue of options — Google Home's schedule timeline (9) and Ring's drawn motion zones (19) are both edited on a picture of the thing, and I had to force them into Flat list and Grouped sections. scope conflates who a change affects with where it is stored, which makes 'This device' the fallback for OS settings that partly sync; VS Code's user/workspace cascade also has no home here (the settings entry has Override layers for exactly this, but the archetype does not). application is pick-one and several surfaces mix immediate fields with saved ones (Notion), so I coded the dominant behaviour.

Two codebook faults drove most of this entry: Grouped sections and Hierarchical panes cannot be told apart because the Grouped exemplar (macOS System Settings) is itself a sidebar-and-pane, and Flat list vs Grouped sections flips depending on whether the unit is the pane named in the sample or the whole settings app. `application` should be pick any — Notion and most SaaS admin surfaces genuinely mix instant toggles with saved forms.
sonnet: Smart-home device settings (4, 9, 15, 19) are coded scope One configured instance throughout, on the reasoning that the setting reaches exactly that one physical device/room rather than an account-wide or team-wide surface; target for the AWS EC2 launch flow (16) is coded '?' since none of the five options describes provisioning a cloud resource.

Two codebook problems surfaced. (1) `organization`'s Grouped sections and Hierarchical panes don't say whether a persistent sidebar that swaps an inline pane (Notion, GitHub, Word) counts as one level (Grouped) or two (Hierarchical) — I resolved it by whether the list itself is ever left behind (push-navigation) versus staying visible beside the swapped pane, but the gloss doesn't say this and the codebook's own macOS System Settings example is structurally identical to the Notion/GitHub cases raters split on. (2) `scope`'s This device / This account everywhere / One configured instance doesn't name smart-home hardware: 'This device' is glossed as the app's own local install, not the physical unit being controlled, and 'One configured instance' is glossed as a saved, portable build (a car configuration) rather than live control of a fixed piece of hardware — both readings are stretches for Hue/Nest/Sonos/Ring.

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Discrete variants: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer
Materials and finishes: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer
Personalization marks: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer

2D composite image: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer
AR on body or room: IKEA Place — Furniture in your room

Free combination: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer
IKEA Place — Furniture in your room

Start from a template: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer

Add to cart: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer

Solo: IKEA Place — Furniture in your room
Community gallery remix: Nike By You — Air Force 1 customizer

fable: Commit as pick-one conflates price feedback with the purchase action; I coded the terminal action where one exists and Live price update only where there is no cart (Tesla kept as the codebook's example). Preview: I code Tesla as 2D composites from product knowledge, against the codebook's example.

commit conflates live price feedback with the terminal action — nearly every priced configurator holds Live price update plus one of Add to cart or Save configuration, so the sub wants pick any. Discrete variants and Materials and finishes overlap on colour (Nike colours vs Tesla paint). order's Any-order panel and Start from a base model co-occur in every car and laptop configurator. preview's exemplars are misassigned: Tesla shows pre-rendered angles, not a manipulable 3D model.
opus: The codebook covered this sample without gaps, which is unsurprising since Tesla and Nike By You are both exemplars and archetypes of the form. commit is the sub that fights the sample: nearly every configurator does several of these at once (live price, save, add to cart), and I coded the flow's terminal act, taking Live price update only where the price is the running feedback and the purchase is a later step. preview's 2D composite versus Realtime 3D is the call most likely to split raters, because several customizers have quietly moved from composited flats to rotatable renders (Nike, Xbox). order's Start from a base model and Start from a template are nearly the same act — the difference is whether the starting point is a product SKU or a designed layout — and I used the template only where the starting artefact is itself a design.

Two sub-dimensions carry most of the disagreement because each asks two questions at once: `order` mixes where a build starts with what sequence is imposed (a Dell page is both a base model and a free panel), and `commit` mixes how price behaves with what act ends the flow (live price and add-to-cart are both true of nearly every commerce configurator) — both should be pick any. The codebook also contradicts itself on Tesla, naming it under Any-order panel while glossing Start-from-a-base-model as 'car trim then options', and its preview scale has no slot for the pre-rendered 360 spin set that most car and sneaker configurators actually ship.
sonnet: commit and collaboration sometimes both plausibly apply (e.g. a save code that is also shareable); coded to the single most distinctively-described action per instance since both subs are pick-one.

Two patterns of miss on my part, not codebook problems: (1) I under-coded `options` as pick-one-ish by naming only the most salient variant type per product and missing genuine secondary axes (add-on packages, finish choices) that were plainly present once named — a pick-any sub-dimension wants the fuller list. (2) For `order`, I initially treated Dell's and Lenovo's section-revealed flow as generic Progressive disclosure while defaulting other, similarly-structured build flows to Any-order or Start-from-a-base-model somewhat inconsistently; the codebook's own Dell exemplar for Progressive disclosure is worth restating in the gloss so raters apply it to look-alike laptop configurators (Lenovo) rather than defaulting to Start-from-a-base-model.

entries.sample: iOS/macOS Settings, Android Settings, VS Code, Slack, GitHub and major SaaS admin.
entries.unit: One settings surface for one product or OS.
usage: Most people change a handful of settings and never return
Power users live in search and JSON
questions: Should every in-product toggle also appear in the settings index?
How do personal and admin layers resolve conflicts visibly?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Timing as pick-one hides that OS settings are mostly instant with a few restart-required items; I coded the dominant behaviour. Drill-down vs Tabbed categories is a judgement for sidebar-plus-pane layouts (macOS, Windows coded Drill-down for their nested panes).

ia's Command-palette jump is a discovery route filed as an information architecture; sidebar-and-pane layouts split Tabbed categories, Sectioned page and Drill-down hierarchy with no rule for depth. safety's No confirm reads two ways: absence of a confirmation dialog (then almost every surface has it) or instant apply (then Save-button surfaces do not). scope lacks a value for a setting that lands on a paired device.
opus: timing is the sub that most needed a value it does not have: four instances are 'mostly instant, a few requiring a restart or sign-out', and pick-one forces the dominant case, so Restart required will probably never be coded by anyone even though the behaviour is common. ia's Sectioned page and Drill-down hierarchy are hard to separate for web settings with a left menu of pages — I followed the codebook's GitHub exemplar for Sectioned page and drilled elsewhere, which is my likeliest disagreement. discovery is close to unobservable in one respect: whether a product has a settings search is a detail that has changed recently for several of these (Discord, Steam, Instagram all added one), so it is a moving target. safety's No confirm co-occurs with everything, since it describes most rows in every surface; it would be more useful as 'nothing here is guarded'. The sample has no instance of Guest without save or Per-profile switch.

Most of this entry's disagreement is a pick-any depth difference rather than a conflict: on `controls`, `discovery` and `safety` the three of us named the same things and one rater simply stopped at what the sample note stated. The one real codebook gap is in `safety`: there is no value for 'a Save button commits it, but nothing warns you', so raters split over whether to call that No confirm at all.
sonnet: ia is coded using a three-way distinction inferred from the codebook's own examples: Sectioned page for single-level web settings reached by separate page navigations (GitHub, Chrome, X); Tabbed categories for a persistent dialog or full-screen overlay whose content swaps in place without navigating away (Slack, Notion, Zoom, Discord, Steam, MS365, Gmail); Drill-down hierarchy reserved for genuinely multi-level navigation (OS settings apps, and mobile apps whose sections push their own sub-screens).

Three codebook problems recurred. (1) `ia`'s Sectioned page and Drill-down hierarchy don't distinguish a persistent sidebar that swaps an inline pane (GitHub, X/Twitter web settings) from true push-navigation between screens — the same ambiguity as the configure archetype's organization sub, and worth a shared fix. (2) `scope` has no value for a settings surface hosted on one device that configures a different, paired device (Apple Watch via the iPhone app) — Device-local is glossed as on-device prefs, and this is neither that nor account-wide; I hold +Paired device unresolved since no other rater independently proposed it. (3) `safety`'s No confirm is ambiguous for admin surfaces that gate every change behind an explicit Save button but never ask 'are you sure' — that is neither instant/no-confirm nor a destructive confirmation, and both readings (opus's inclusion, fable's/my exclusion) are defensible from the gloss as written.

Synced across devices: Apple Music — Now Playing on Mac

recorded.name: Metadata overlay
recorded.gloss: Cast, music and trivia about the current scene shown over the video on pause or hover (Prime Video X-Ray)

recorded.name: Resizable app window
recorded.gloss: The player is an ordinary desktop window the person sizes and moves — neither embedded in a page, nor fullscreen, nor a miniature persistent bar

recorded.name: Contextual info overlay
recorded.gloss: A panel of contextual metadata about the currently playing moment (cast, music, trivia) is shown alongside the video, distinct from captions, end cards, live chat, ad breaks, or ambient lyrics/visuals

fable: resume: 'Synced across devices' was reserved for live position hand-off (Spotify Connect, Whispersync, iCloud podcasts); cross-session resume that also works on another device (Netflix, Plex, YouTube) was coded Resume position because the Netflix exemplar sits there. Transcripts were coded under 'Lyrics synced to time' as the only synced-text variation.
opus: The teaching players (Coursera, Panopto, Khan) all pair the video with a synchronised transcript or slide list that is the real navigation device, and neither position nor overlays has a value for it; I coded Captions and noted the gap each time. mode also conflates framing with device state — YouTube's watch page is an inline embed, a theater mode and a PiP depending on what you press, so I coded the resting state.
sonnet: mode was a poor fit for standalone desktop file players (VLC, QuickTime) since 'a resizable primary window that can go fullscreen' isn't quite inline-embed, theater, fullscreen-as-default, mini/PiP, or lock-screen; marked QuickTime '?' and picked the closest (Fullscreen) for VLC given its movie-watching framing in the sample.

Three codebook problems surfaced here: `resume` is pick-one but conflates whether playback resumes with where the position is stored, so Resume position and Synced across devices overlap and every syncing product forces an arbitrary choice; `mode`'s 'Lock-screen / Now Playing' reads as both the system lock-screen surface and any app's full-screen Now Playing screen, which split all three raters on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, YouTube Music and Audible; and a time-synced transcript (Apple Podcasts, Coursera, Panopto) has no code at all — 'Lyrics synced to time' under `position` wants generalising to time-synced text.

entries.name: Playlist and queue
entries.definition: An ordered list of media items that defines what plays now and what comes after, editable during consumption.

dimensions.name: Queue structure
dimensions.question: How is the upcoming sequence structured?

values.name: Manual queue over a context
values.description: Queue sits on top of an album or playlist

values.name: Rule-built playlist
values.description: The list is generated and maintained by a saved rule — these podcasts, sorted this way, this many episodes — and refills itself as new items arrive; neither hand-ordered nor algorithmically seeded

dimensions.name: Editing the order
dimensions.question: How does a person change what comes next?

dimensions.name: Order policy
dimensions.question: Who decides the order when the person does not?

dimensions.name: Item representation
dimensions.question: What does each queued item show?

values.name: Tempo and key
values.description: DJ software shows BPM, musical key and beat-grid state per track, which decide what can be mixed next

dimensions.name: Queue surface
dimensions.question: Where is the queue shown?

dimensions.name: Persistence
dimensions.question: Does the queue survive across sessions and devices?

wild.note: Manual queue edits are common; policies for when autoplay may interrupt a queue are rarely exposed.

examples.name: Spotify
examples.note: Play Next, Add to Queue, reorder

techniques.name: Queue rules
techniques.how: Make autoplay and shuffle into editable rules with priority over the manual queue (“finish album, then radio”).

techniques.name: Surface then reorder
techniques.how: Any surfaced attribute (energy, BPM, duration left) becomes a sort key for the remaining queue.

techniques.name: Build the night
techniques.how: Describe a listening plan in words; the model proposes a queue with inspectable sources and swap alternatives.

entries.sample: Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, Netflix, podcast apps and DJ software.
entries.unit: One active queue or playlist playback context.
usage: People fight autoplay that inserts over a carefully built queue
questions: Is a queue a sequence pattern specialized from browse-collections?
Should collaborative queues show authorship on every item?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: policy is pick-one but nearly every queue is manual with shuffle/repeat toggles and an autoplay tail; I coded Strict manual order unless autoplay-after-end is on by default (Apple Music, YouTube, YouTube Music, SoundCloud). persistence conflates session/device sync with saving; coded the mechanism the sample names.
opus: policy asks who decides the order when the person does not, but most music queues answer twice: shuffle while the context lasts, then autoplay-similar when it runs out. I coded the toggle the product puts in front of you and noted the tail. surface also has no value for a queue that is never shown (Pandora), which I coded n/a rather than forcing it into Voice readout only.
sonnet: surface was a recurring judgment call between 'Full-screen list' and 'Sheet over player' for mobile up-next screens reached from Now Playing; leaned Sheet over player only where the product frames it as a tab/overlay on the player rather than its own dedicated page.

`policy` is the biggest problem in this entry: it is pick one but asks a question most products answer several ways at once — a hand-built queue with a shuffle toggle and an autoplay-after-end switch is all three at once, which is why opus read every shuffle toggle as Shuffle while fable and I read the same screens as Strict manual order. It wants to be pick any. Two smaller ones: `surface`'s Full-screen list and Sheet over player overlap so far that the codebook's own Full-screen list exemplar (the Spotify Queue sheet) is a sheet over the player, and `surface` has no value for a queue rendered as a section of an ordinary page (Netflix's season list); `persistence` has no value for a queue that survives relaunch on one device but does not sync (Apple Music Up Next).

Annotations become a personal index of the book

How do shared highlights interact with personal ones?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Typeface choice: Google Play Books — Reading a book
Size and spacing: Google Play Books — Reading a book
Light dark sepia: Google Play Books — Reading a book

Reflowable ebook: Google Play Books — Reading a book
Fixed layout: Adobe Acrobat Reader — Reading a PDF

Table of contents: Google Play Books — Reading a book

Search in book: Google Play Books — Reading a book

recorded.name: Estimated total read time
recorded.gloss: A fixed reading-time estimate is shown up front for the whole piece (e.g., '6 min read'), rather than a dynamically tracked location, percent remaining, time left in the current chapter, a daily goal, or a streak

fable: progress is n/a for reading modes and article apps that track nothing (Safari, Firefox, NYT, Medium, Wikipedia, Substack). Ebook apps mix an in-book indicator with app-level goals; I coded the in-book indicator unless the sample named goals (Play Books).
opus: progress is n/a for six of twenty: reader modes and news apps show nothing at all about where you are, and Location only overstates it. The web and article readers also make navigation systematically empty — there is no table of contents, scrubber or in-work search in a single article — which is a real finding rather than a coding failure, but it means half this entry's cells are empty arrays.
sonnet: progress defaulted to 'Location only' for most simple article/one-off readers (Safari, Firefox, NYT, Wikipedia, Substack, Matter's peers, Vision Pro Safari, Speechify, Wattpad) since none of the samples described a percent, chapter-time, goal, or streak mechanism for them.

Two structural problems. `pagination` mixes two axes: Reflowable ebook describes how text is laid out while Paginated pages and Continuous scroll describe how it is chunked, so an EPUB that reflows into page turns is two values at once (this alone split all three raters on Apple Books). `progress` is pick one but products report several at once — Kobo shows both time left in chapter and a percentage, Libby likewise — and it has no value for pages left in a chapter (adopted here as a proposal), for a static 'six minute read' estimate, or for a listening progress bar in a text-to-speech reader; it also lacks a clean way to say a reading surface tracks nothing at all, which is why Safari and Firefox Reader, the NYT, Wikipedia, Substack and Medium all had to be coded n/a.

entries.name: Stories

dimensions.name: Frame content
dimensions.question: What can a frame hold?

dimensions.question: How are authors ordered in the tray?

values.name: 48-hour expiry

dimensions.name: Presentation
dimensions.question: How is the story experienced on screen?

values.name: On a profile
values.description: Stories live on a profile page (highlight circles under the bio, a status behind the avatar) rather than in a tray, tab or column

wild.note: Close Friends and hide-from lists exist; timer length and tray ranking are almost never user-tunable.

examples.name: Instagram
examples.note: Close Friends and hide story from

techniques.name: Pace the timer
techniques.how: Let people set default dwell time and tap-skip size as a personal stories pace, separate from feed scroll speed.

techniques.name: Tray as overview
techniques.how: Surface why an author is high in the tray and allow pin, mute and regroup by attribute (mutuals, brands, news).

techniques.name: Catch me up
techniques.how: Summarize unseen stories from selected authors with links back to each frame before they expire.

entries.sample: Instagram, Snapchat, WhatsApp Status, Facebook Stories and TikTok Stories.
entries.unit: One author stack viewed in one session.
usage: People binge a tray then feel behind when new rings appear
questions: Are stories a sequence media-player or a specialized feed?
Should expiry be a personal preference as well as an author choice?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

No expiry: Google Web Stories — Publisher web story

Public web: Google Web Stories — Publisher web story

Full-bleed vertical: Google Web Stories — Publisher web story

recorded.name: Permanent page
recorded.gloss: The frames never expire: the story is a durable page or artefact (a publisher URL, a yearly recap, a generated memory) that happens to use the story form

recorded.name: Tied to profile picture
recorded.gloss: A single ambient status is shown behind or attached to a person's profile picture itself, rather than in a feed tray, a standalone tab, inline in the chat list, or a desktop column

fable: presentation was read as where the stories live (tray, tab, column, profile) since three of its five variations are entry points; 'Full-bleed vertical' was kept for stacks with no home surface. ordering is unobservable from memory for VK, Twitch and LINE.
opus: The pattern assumes an author tray, an expiry and an audience, and four instances (Web Stories, Wrapped, Memories, and Highlights to a lesser degree) borrow the story grammar without any of the three — hence two proposals and several n/a in ordering. presentation also mixes the playback surface with where stories live in the app: Full-bleed vertical is true of every mobile instance, so I used it only where nothing more specific applied and coded the tray, tab or chat-list home otherwise.
sonnet: presentation required a consistent rule since the codebook cites Instagram for two different values (Full-bleed vertical and Tray above feed): coded the product's structural home for stories (tray-in-feed vs standalone tab vs inline-in-chat vs desktop split) where that distinction was the more informative fact, and Full-bleed vertical only for single-author/personal experiences with no such structural placement (Web Stories, Highlights, Wrapped, Memories).

`presentation` is the entry's real problem: it is pick one but its five values sit on two axes — Full-bleed vertical describes how a frame plays, while Tray above feed, Standalone status tab, Inline in chat list and Desktop column describe where you enter from — and the codebook itself cites Instagram for two of them, which is why the three raters split on Snapchat, TikTok, Telegram, Signal, Highlights and Memories. It wants to be pick any, or to be split into two sub-dimensions. `ordering` has the same shape at a smaller scale: unseen-first is a layer over a chronological or ranked base order, so 'Unseen first' swallows almost every tray if read strictly. Two smaller findings: `lifetime`'s 24-hour expiry hard-codes a duration that Twitch (48h) and Telegram (6/12/24/48h, selectable) do not share — one 'fixed expiry window' variation carrying the duration would fix it — and `audience` has no value for 'everyone on this platform' short of the open web (Snapchat Discover, Telegram's default Everyone), nor for a story with no audience at all until it is shared (adopted here as +Just me).

entries.name: Create and compose
entries.definition: Make an artifact by directly manipulating its parts: text, shapes, nodes, clips or code.

dimensions.name: Surface
dimensions.question: What kind of space holds the artifact?

values.name: 3D scene
values.description: A navigable three-dimensional space with a camera, where the artifact is objects in depth rather than marks on a plane — the surface of every 3D, CAD and XR authoring tool

dimensions.name: Object structure
dimensions.question: How are parts organized?

dimensions.name: Selection
dimensions.question: What can be acted on at once?

dimensions.name: Tool access
dimensions.question: How are tools reached?

values.name: Command palette
values.description: A searchable launcher for every command in the tool, opened by a shortcut and driven by typing the action's name; distinct from a toolbar, a contextual toolbar and from slash commands, which insert content into a document

dimensions.name: Generation
dimensions.question: How much does the tool make for you?

dimensions.name: Authorship
dimensions.question: How many people make it, and how?

wild.note: Creative professionals routinely customize workspaces, toolbars, shortcuts and plugins.

techniques.name: Attributes as objects
techniques.how: Styles and properties become first-class objects that can be applied, linked and searched, after Object-Oriented Drawing (Xia et al. CHI '16), which CHI '25 builds on.

techniques.name: Select by attribute
techniques.how: Form and operate on aggregate selections by shared attribute values, after Collection Objects (Xia et al. CHI '17).

techniques.name: Variations of this
techniques.how: Generate alternatives for the selection, laid out side by side as a small design space to compare and blend.

entries.sample: Top creative, design, office and developer tools on desktop and web.
entries.unit: One authoring environment for one artifact type.
usage: Experts rebuild their workspace on every new machine
questions: Is there a shared grammar under documents, canvases, graphs and timelines?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Object structure has no value for source-text editors (coded n/a) and only Flat objects for flowing rich text; Authorship coded by where the file lives (desktop file → Solo even where cloud co-authoring is possible).

generation is pick-one but nearly every office and design tool holds Templates and a prompt feature at once; the Canva Magic Design example shows the codebook wants the highest level shipped, and the gloss should say so or the sub-dimension should be pick any. authorship has the same hybrid problem for desktop apps that co-author through the cloud. structure has no value for flowing rich text, and slide tools (groups and z-order, no layers panel) fall between Flat objects and Layers and groups. Selection's Text range needs a rule for character ranges inside a text object in a canvas tool.
opus: Structure has no variation for a flowing text document: paragraphs had to be called Blocks, which blurs the line with Notion, and source text had to be n/a. Generation is also a pick-one over features that coexist — almost every tool now has templates and a prompt — so I coded the strongest thing the product ships in that surface and said so in each note.

generation is a pick-one over rungs that coexist — almost every tool here ships templates and a prompt — so I re-coded it with one stated rule: take the affordance the sampler put on the screen, and where the screen is silent take the strongest rung that ships to an ordinary user without a separate purchase or plugin. It wants to be pick any. structure still has no variation for flowing text (paragraphs had to be Blocks) and its Layers and groups compounds two independent things: a persistent layer stack and grouping — the split on Keynote and PowerPoint was entirely that. Slash commands is named for a character rather than a behaviour, which leaves Google Docs' @ menu uncodeable.
sonnet: Object structure didn't fit raw source-text tools (VS Code, Overleaf) at all — code isn't organized as flat/layered/component/block/node parts — coded '?' for those two. 'Blocks' was stretched to cover ordinary flowing-paragraph documents (Word/Docs/Obsidian), not just literal block editors like Notion.

Generation is pick-one but Google Docs and Notion each truthfully hold Templates and Generate-from-a-prompt at once (a gallery plus a bolted-on AI writer); I took the codebook's first-listed value each time, but the sub-dimension wants to be pick-any. Authorship's Real-time multiplayer doesn't distinguish always-on multiplayer (Figma, Notion) from collaboration that's conditional on cloud storage (Word, PowerPoint, Keynote), which is why raters split product-by-product on whether to code the default solo state or the available collaborative one.

entries.name: Canvas editor

dimensions.name: Canvas model
dimensions.question: What kind of space is it?

dimensions.name: Object hierarchy
dimensions.question: How are objects nested and reused?

dimensions.name: Selection
dimensions.question: How are objects selected?

dimensions.name: Tools
dimensions.question: How are tools reached?

dimensions.name: Generation
dimensions.question: What does the tool make for you?

dimensions.name: Multiplayer
dimensions.question: How is working together shown?

dimensions.name: Responsiveness
dimensions.question: How do designs respond to size?

wild.note: Designers customize panels, plugins, shortcuts and libraries routinely.

techniques.name: Attributes as objects
techniques.how: Fills, strokes and effects become objects that can be dragged onto shapes, linked and edited in one place (Object-Oriented Drawing, CHI '16).

techniques.name: Select by attribute
techniques.how: Gather everything sharing a value into a live collection and operate on it (Collection Objects, CHI '17).

techniques.name: Variations side by side
techniques.how: Generate alternatives of a selected frame along chosen dimensions, spread as a grid like Meridian’s Design Space view.

entries.sample: Design, whiteboard, presentation and diagramming tools.
usage: Designers duplicate frames to explore instead of using version history
questions: Can generated variations stay linked to the source so edits propagate?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

recorded.name: Variations to choose from
recorded.gloss: The tool proposes several ready-made layout options built from what you already placed, for you to pick one — not a template gallery, not a typed prompt, and more than a small tidy-up (e.g., PowerPoint Designer)

fable: Hierarchy for slide tools (grouping and z-order without a layers panel) falls between Flat objects and Layers and groups, coded Flat; Multiplayer includes Solo as a value inside a pick-any, used alone.

generation is pick-one but most tools hold Templates and a prompt feature; the create entry's gloss asks how much (ordinal, highest wins) while this one asks what kind, so I coded the codebook-named value where the product is named and the front door otherwise, and the two entries should say which they mean. hierarchy conflates nesting (auto-layout) and reuse (components), and slide tools with groups but no layers panel sit between Flat objects and Layers and groups. Live cursors should cover live selections (Sketch).
opus: Hierarchy and responsiveness are pick-one over things that coexist: Figma has constraints and auto layout, Sketch has constraints and Smart Layout, so the code records which one the file is actually built with. Generation also forced a choice between a template library and a prompt in tools that ship both (Miro, FigJam, Canva); I followed the codebook's own examples where it named one.

generation is pick one over rungs that coexist, and this entry's list is also missing the parent entry's Variations to choose from, which is the only honest code for PowerPoint's Designer; I re-coded these with the tie-break of taking the first truthfully-held value, which collapses most modern tools onto Templates — the sub-dimension wants to be pick any. hierarchy has the same problem for Framer (stacks and components are both true) and its Layers and groups compounds a persistent layer stack with plain grouping, which is what split the three slide editors. multiplayer lists Solo inside a pick any alongside values it excludes, so an unshared document and a shared one cannot be told apart cleanly.
sonnet: Multiplayer/collaboration is often a capability the sampled screen doesn't show directly; I coded from general product knowledge of each tool's collaboration model rather than only the note.

Hierarchy and generation are pick-one but Framer truthfully holds two values at once on both (Auto-layout containers and Components with overrides; Templates and Layouts from a prompt) — I took the codebook's first-listed value each time. Generation's list is shorter than the parent create archetype's and has no equivalent to create's own 'Variations to choose from', which is what PowerPoint Designer actually does; +Variations to choose from proposes closing that gap rather than stretching Templates, Layouts from a prompt or Tidying assistance to fit.

entries.name: Code editor
entries.definition: Reading and writing source code with structure-aware tools around the text.

dimensions.name: Code representation
dimensions.question: What is shown alongside the text?

values.name: Projections
values.description: Alternative views that edit the same code

dimensions.name: Workspace layout
dimensions.question: How is the workspace arranged?

dimensions.name: Commands
dimensions.question: How are actions invoked?

dimensions.name: Assistance
dimensions.question: How much does the editor write?

dimensions.name: Change review
dimensions.question: How are changes reviewed?

dimensions.name: Collaboration
dimensions.question: How do people code together?

dimensions.name: Customization depth
dimensions.question: How far can the editor be changed?

wild.note: Among the most customized software there is.

techniques.name: Projections
techniques.how: Show a piece of code as a table, a form or a diagram that edits the same source (Lorgnette, UIST '23, cited by Meridian).

techniques.name: Settings as a shareable spec
techniques.how: A workspace’s layout, keybindings and extensions export as one file others can apply.

techniques.name: Explain this change
techniques.how: Every AI edit arrives as hunks with a rationale per hunk to accept or reject.

entries.sample: Desktop IDEs, browser-based editors and notebooks’ code cells.
usage: Developers carry their configuration between machines as dotfiles
questions: What is the overview–detail structure of code, and can it be made malleable like an ODI?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Change review's Diff in the gutter is hard to recall for browser editors (three ?); Depth's Extensions vs Settings depends on whether an editor-extension marketplace exists, which is fuzzy for notebooks and cloud IDEs.

collab is pick-one but the codebook's own example (VS Code Live Share) is an add-on, so the sub-dimension must mean capability rather than default mode; it should say so, or become pick any with Solo dropped. review's Diff in the gutter conflates where a diff shows with reviewing a diff at all (Magit); browser editors without gutter marks all fall to Save only. Zen mode and command palette availability in smaller editors (Zed, Arduino IDE 2) are hard to recall reliably.
opus: Assistance and representation were easy; review and depth were not. Review conflates a version-control display with a model-change gate, so an autosaving web editor with a separate git pane (Replit, RStudio) has to read as Save only. Projections finally earned its keep on the IDEs with visual designers (Xcode, Android Studio, Visual Studio), which is worth keeping in the codebook.

Most of this entry's disagreement was a pick any coded short rather than a conflict, so the packet reads as one rater listing fewer true items. Two glosses caused real trouble: Panels is glossed by function (terminal and problems) but read by chrome, which is what split Neovim and Emacs; and Change review conflates review inside the editor with an external git client, so Magit and RStudio's git pane have to be called Save only while Sublime's gutter marks count. Customization depth also has no way to say that a product retired its extension system, and collab has no way to say 'bundled' versus 'a marketplace install', which is the only thing separating Code With Me from Live Share.
sonnet: Collab defaulted to Solo whenever the sampled screen didn't specifically show a shared/live-editing feature, even for products (Colab, Replit, Zed) where I know real-time collaboration exists as a named capability, which I did credit.

I under-coded almost every pick-any sub-dimension in this entry on the first pass — representation, layout, commands and assistance are all 'pick any that apply' lists, and I consistently picked only the single most salient item per product instead of checking the whole variation list against what I actually know of each tool; fable and opus's near-total agreement with each other across this entry reflects thoroughness, not a codebook problem. The one real codebook-adjacent finding: review's four values (Save only / Diff in the gutter / Accept or reject hunks / Pull request review) have no value for 'agent changes reviewed in a chat thread with checkpoint rollback' (Replit), which is neither a gutter diff nor a hunk-level accept/reject bar — I coded it Save only for lack of a closer fit, but a future round might want a value for chat-mediated review.

techniques.name: Views of one document

entries.sample: Office suites, note apps, publishing and scholarly writing tools.
entries.unit: One editor for one document type.
usage: Writers outline in one view and draft in another
questions: Can a document keep one source while each reader sees their own structure?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: Writing assistance coded for what the editor itself ships (browser spellcheck and paid AI add-ons excluded), which leaves many empty arrays; OneNote's free-form containers fit no document model.

assistance needs a rule for bundled AI: Gemini, Copilot, Notion AI, Atlassian Intelligence and Writing Tools are now included in the plans the editor is sold in, so 'what the editor ships' has to count them, and browser spellcheck versus an in-app spellcheck setting needs the same rule. page's Pageless versus Fixed reading column should be glossed by whether there is a fixed measure. access should say whether hardware-keyboard shortcuts count for a mobile instance.
opus: Tracking is pick-one over mechanisms that coexist — Google Docs has suggestion mode and version history, Word has both too — so the code records the stronger one and loses the other. Assistance also cannot distinguish help the editor ships from the operating system's (Apple Intelligence in Pages and Notes) or the browser's spellcheck, which I counted as absent.

Most of this entry's disagreement was about where writing help comes from, so I re-coded assistance with one rule: count what the editor itself ships, not a paid AI add-on (Copilot, Gemini, Atlassian Intelligence, Craft AI) and not an OS-level service that appears in every text field (Apple's Writing Tools). Two glosses caused the rest: Outline sidebar is named for a desktop sidebar, so a mobile app that opens the same outline as a panel cannot be coded without argument; and Focus mode's gloss says 'dims everything but the sentence', which excludes block-granularity spotlights like WordPress's. Reading modes is also pick one over values that coexist — Obsidian and Typora each truthfully hold two — so I used the earlier-listed value as the tie-break.
sonnet: Tracking defaulted to None for personal note apps with no named versioning/suggestion feature, even where informal undo history exists.

I systematically missed native, non-AI baseline features across this entry — OS-level spellcheck (assistance), a product's own keyboard shortcuts, and named version-history features (tracking) — because I was looking for the single most distinctive fact about each product rather than checking the full pick-any list. Two separate codebook-adjacent findings: (1) modes' Focus mode gloss ('dims everything but the sentence') describes iA Writer's specific implementation; Scrivener's Composition mode is the same general category of full-screen distraction-free writing without doing sentence-level dimming, and the gloss should generalise. (2) 'Assistance' and 'generation'-style dimensions keep splitting raters on whether a real but paid/opt-in AI feature (Copilot, Notion AI, Atlassian Intelligence, Apple Intelligence) counts if it's reached from inside the editor itself — I've resolved this round by crediting it whenever it's native to the product's own UI, regardless of pricing tier, the same standard I used for code-editor's Copilot-based cells.
