coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Number only: Google Search Console — Total clicks tile

recorded.gloss: The value is drawn as a ring or arc — progress toward a goal, or a 0–100 score in a coloured band — which is how nearly every health and fitness tile encodes its number; neither a sparkline nor a bullet chart

recorded.name: Plots on the shared chart

opus: Context and encoding overlap by design (Sparkline is a value in both), so a tile with a trend line is coded twice for the same fact. Neither dimension can express threshold or conditional colour, which is the whole point of a Grafana stat panel or a Datadog query value; and Fixed vs Chosen per tile is only distinguishable when the tile carries its own range control.

entries.name: Toast
entries.definition: A brief, non-blocking message about the outcome of an action that goes away on its own.

dimensions.name: Duration
dimensions.question: How long does it stay?

dimensions.name: Content
dimensions.question: What does it carry?

dimensions.name: Position
dimensions.question: Where does it appear?

values.name: Bottom right stack
values.description: Cards slide in and stack in the lower-right corner (VS Code notifications, sonner-style dashboards)

values.name: Centre of screen
values.description: A pill or HUD in the middle of the screen over the content, in the manner of Apple's Music/volume HUDs

values.name: Centre overlay
values.description: A pill or HUD floating at the centre of the screen over the content, the iOS system-confirmation shape; not anchored to an edge or to the control that caused it

dimensions.name: Severity
dimensions.question: What kind of outcome is it?

wild.note: Duration and position are fixed; missed toasts are simply gone.

techniques.name: Toast history
techniques.how: Missed toasts can be reopened from a small history, and a person can lengthen the duration everywhere.

entries.sample: Web and mobile apps with action feedback.
usage: Screen-reader and slow readers miss auto-dismissing messages
questions: Should error messages ever be toasts?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

recorded.name: Screen centre
recorded.gloss: A brief confirmation pill appears vertically centred on screen rather than anchored to an edge — an Apple HUD-style toast

fable: Position lacks bottom right, the commonest corner for desktop toast libraries; Severity for a system with several variants was coded by its default (Neutral) and noted.

content's Message only reads as exclusive but one rater lists it beside Action on every Undo toast, which is all of the content disagreement; position omits bottom right and the screen-centre HUD, and duration is pick one over toasts that both auto-dismiss and pause on hover.
opus: Duration mixes three different questions — how long it stays, whether hovering holds it, and whether several are shown at once — so Queued and Pause while hovered could not be coded from product knowledge and stacking behaviour (Linear, Vercel, VS Code) had no place to go. Severity is Neutral for almost everything, since most toasts acknowledge a small action rather than report an outcome.

Most of this packet is one codebook fault: 'Message only' is named as an exclusive ('only') but sits in a pick-any list, so a rater can read it either as 'carries a message' or as 'carries nothing else'. It should be renamed Message, or the gloss should say it excludes Action. 'Duration' has the same shape of problem — Pause while hovered entails Auto-dismiss rather than competing with it.
sonnet: Severity: I treated routine housekeeping confirmations (archived, saved, copied, added) as Neutral to match the codebook's own 'Archived' example, reserving Success for outcomes with real stakes (payment/post/issue creation).

Content's 'Message only' reads as pick-any but is really an exclusivity flag (no action/icon/progress present); I over-applied it in round 1 to every toast that also had an action. The codebook could gloss it as 'no other content present' to head this off. Also a three-way naming split on the same missing centre-screen position (three different names for one gap) is itself a codebook finding, not a coding disagreement.

recorded.name: In-content links
recorded.gloss: Following a hyperlink embedded within the body content itself (article prose, a related-stories module), not a structured navigation menu, search box or command palette.

fable: responsive names sidebars only; top bars that fold into a hamburger (GitHub, NYT) were coded Sidebar becomes drawer. Single-form-factor systems (XR, voice) got n/a.

responsive assumes every product starts from a sidebar, so top-bar sites and split views each needed a proposal; routes has no value for links inside content, the main route on the networked web; architecture is pick one but a flat shell can hold a sequence (Uber), and depth's Mixed swallows most products with a sidebar.
opus: architecture is pick-one over products that are plainly two structures at once: Uber is flat tabs wrapped around a sequential booking flow, GOV.UK a hierarchy wrapped around sequential services, Amazon a hierarchy refined by facets. I coded the persistent structure and named the other in the note. depth is the weakest sub-dimension here — every large product is Mixed, and the three variations do not distinguish a file system from a SaaS app. The voice and XR instances also strain placement and responsive, which both presuppose a screen.

responsive is pick one but holds two values at once for any product with three breakpoints (YouTube and Windows 11 Settings are both a rail at medium AND tabs/drawer at narrow) — it wants to be pick any; I took the earlier-listed variation and said so. Its four variations also all presuppose a sidebar, which is why three instances needed +Top bar collapses to a menu button. 'Address' reads as 'this is on the web' unless the gloss's word 'readable' is enforced; I enforced it (Amazon's title slugs count, Netflix's numeric ids do not) and that is where most of the cues disagreement sat. placement's 'None' glosses as 'content links only', so it cannot be used for XR, where the navigation surface exists but is summoned by hardware. Finally, sonnet and I proposed the same routes variation under two names — my '+Content links' and sonnet's '+In-content links' are one variation and should merge; I kept 'Content links' because the codebook already uses that phrase in placement's None gloss.
sonnet: The responsive dimension's four fixed variations are all built around a sidebar transforming; every top-bar-based site in this sample (Amazon, Netflix, GitHub, NYT) hit that same gap, which is why one proposal covers all four rather than four separate one-off guesses. XR instances (10, 11) also stretched 'placement' and got a matching proposal; I left cues as '?' there rather than invent specifics I don't confidently know.

techniques.how: Hide the shell for a task and bring it back on intent, remembered per destination.

techniques.how: “Set up my sidebar for the launch” proposes pinned items and sections as a reviewable change.

entries.sample: Top 50 productivity, communication and media apps on web, desktop and mobile.
entries.unit: One product’s shell on one platform.
usage: People collapse chrome during deep work and restore it to switch
questions: How much shell structure can be personal before shared help and screenshots stop matching?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Navigation rail: Microsoft Outlook — New Outlook for Windows

Mini-apps inside an app: Microsoft Outlook — New Outlook for Windows

recorded.name: Sibling apps in one shell
recorded.gloss: One product's shell carries a second, whole first-party application beside its own sections — Gmail's Mail/Meet bottom bar, the Calendar/Keep/Tasks side strip — which is neither a single app nor the sandboxed third-party mini-program platform 'Mini-apps inside an app' describes

fable: narrowing is n/a for phone apps (already the narrowest); Jira was coded on its 2025 sidebar navigation rather than the sample's top bar.

primary and secondary do not say whether an icon rail beside a channel column is a sidebar or a rail, which is why Discord and Teams split; Workspace switcher needs to say whether an account or profile switcher counts; narrowing needs an explicit rule for shells sampled on the phone (n/a) versus coding the desktop counterpart.
opus: secondary has no variation for a bottom bar that switches between sibling products in one shell (Gmail's Mail/Meet), and structure cannot describe a shell that hosts other first-party apps in a side panel (Gmail's Calendar/Keep/Tasks strip, Teams' and Outlook's pinnable apps) short of calling them mini-apps, which overstates it. narrowing I read as naming the form the shell takes when narrow, so phone-only instances take the variation that matches their own layout rather than n/a.

narrowing has no 'Unchanged' variation, so a shell that is the same at every width can only be recorded as n/a — that single gap produced a quarter of this entry's disagreement (instances 5, 7, 9, 11, 16), and it also tempts raters to restate `primary` instead. It is pick one but several shells do two things at once (Discord becomes bottom tabs AND keeps a channel drawer); it wants to be pick any. secondary's 'Second sidebar column' presupposes a first sidebar, so a product with a top bar and one sub-destination column (Jira) has nowhere clean to go. structure asks 'how many applications does one shell hold' but offers only 'Mini-apps inside an app' for any answer above one, which is why the three of us split three ways on Gmail, Teams and Outlook.
sonnet: 'narrowing' was the hardest sub-dimension to apply honestly for shells I know mainly at one screen size: already-mobile instances got 'n/a' (nothing further to describe), while desktop apps I don't use daily (Figma, New Outlook) got '?' rather than a guessed breakpoint behaviour.

entries.sample: Developer tools, design tools and SaaS products with a keyboard palette, plus OS launchers.

questions: Can the palette be the discovery surface for a whole malleable interface’s customizations?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

adopted.name: Prompt line at the bottom edge

fable: Arguments is pick-one but most palettes mix commands that run at once with ones that open a follow-up list; I coded whichever the palette is known for. Emacs' minibuffer is neither a toolbar nor an overlay.

arguments is pick one but every real palette mixes commands that run at once with a few that open a follow-up list, so it wants a which-dominates rule; detail cannot hold a shortcut and a description together (Google Docs); types lacks people and code symbols.
opus: detail is pick-one over palettes that show two things at once — IntelliJ and Notion give both a location and a shortcut — and ranking is genuinely unobservable in several cases, since fuzzy scoring and recency weighting are combined behind one ordered list; I coded whichever the product is known for and said so. types also blurs Places and Objects wherever a page is both.

Two pick-one subs are doing pick-any work, and they account for most of this packet. detail asks which of four things a row shows when IntelliJ shows a location and a shortcut and Windows shows rows and a panel; arguments asks how a command collects input when every general-purpose palette runs most commands immediately and nests a few. I resolved both by taking the codebook's first-listed value, but both subs want to be pick any (or to ask about the palette's dominant case explicitly). The third fault is types: Places and Objects and files overlap wherever a page, a channel or a person is both a thing and a destination, which is the whole of the Notion and Slack disagreement — and Sonnet's +People and +Code symbols are both symptoms of that list being a list of six examples rather than a partition.
sonnet: Detail was often a judgment call between Name only and Name and description/shortcut when a result shows secondary text I can't confirm is always present (e.g. path context, category grouping) — I leaned toward the richer value only where I have fairly confident recall.

fable: holds lacks the two commonest map-app contents (results lists) and forms; proposed both. Ride-option sheets were coded Selection detail as the nearest fit.

holds is missing the three commonest map and social contents (lists of options, comment threads, payment forms); dismissBy's Swipe down and Minimize overlap on every sheet with a floor unless Swipe down means removal; Modal with scrim bundles blocking with dimming, which TikTok separates; Peek bar co-occurs with medium and large so detents wants to be pick any or Peek bar wants to mean has a floor.
opus: holds is the thin sub-dimension: four variations cannot cover the sheets that carry search, results, a conversation or a payment, and I had to read comments sheets as selection detail to place them at all. detents also conflates two ideas — how many resting heights there are, and whether the lowest one is still visible — so Peek bar competes with Medium and large rather than sitting beside it.

holds is not a closed set — a bottom sheet can hold anything, and the four variations forced three raters into five different proposals; it should be reframed as pick any over broad content kinds (actions / detail / chooser / thread / form / status / media). detents conflates the number of resting heights with whether the lowest one stays visible, so Peek bar competes with Medium and large instead of sitting beside it; and dismissBy mixes the trigger (swipe, button, outside tap) with the destination (minimize), and 'Tap the scrim' cannot express tapping outside a sheet that has no scrim (TikTok comments).
sonnet: Holds was the dimension with the most genuine coverage gaps — four proposals across the 20 instances, all for recurring content types (comments, map-result lists, tracking, search) rather than one-offs, which suggests the dimension's four variations were drawn mainly from action/detail sheets and didn't anticipate map- and feed-app sheets. dismissBy came back '?' three times for sheets that are more a persistent mode of the screen than something explicitly closed.

opus: Every instance in this sample came out as a Location trail, which says the sample is uniform but also that the type sub-dimension barely discriminates: I read Attribute strictly as a trail built from facets the person chose, so the retail category trails (which the codebook cites as the Attribute example) are Location here — that is the cell most likely to split the three of us. placement also has no variation for a trail that is the page heading itself rather than a line above one, which is what Drive, Dropbox and the AWS console do; I coded those Above the title.
sonnet: Every sampled instance is a Location-type trail with Click-to-go-up as its baseline interaction — genuinely the dominant real-world pattern; History-type (documentation 'how you got here' trails) and Attribute-type (retail filter trails) breadcrumbs exist but are rarer, and I didn't stretch any of these 20 to fit them without real evidence.

fable: Push content vs Docked was the hard line: I used Push for panels that temporarily narrow content and Docked for panels that are part of the layout.

relationship has no value for an overlay that does not dim, and the gap between Push content and Docked (temporary versus part of the layout) is not stated, which is why the record panels split three ways; responsive reuses 'modal' for what relationship calls overlay, so a no-scrim overlay has to be coded 'Always modal'.
opus: relationship has no room for an overlay without a scrim, which is what several right-hand detail panels actually are; I coded those Overlay with scrim and said so. The line between Push content and Docked also has to be drawn by hand — I took Docked to mean the panel is part of the layout and Push to mean it arrives and shoves content over. responsive is an inference for the desktop-only panels, which simply have no narrow form.

relationship had no overlay-without-a-scrim value, which is what most right-hand detail panels actually are — three raters' disagreement on GitHub, Notion and the OS panels is entirely that missing value. responsive then repeats the same axis in different words: its variations name modality (Always modal) rather than adaptation, so a no-scrim overlay that never docks has to be filed as 'modal', and OS panels tempt a rater to n/a. responsive is also ambiguous about what counts as the same drawer at another size (one responsive site, as with Nike, versus a separate mobile skin, as with Wikipedia).
sonnet: Relationship was a frequent judgment call for record/detail panels that neither dim the background nor visibly resize the main content (GitHub Projects, Jira, Linear, Notion, Asana) — I coded these Docked since nothing pushes or scrims, though I can't rule out a light scrim I'm not recalling precisely. The two OS-level panels (Windows Widgets, macOS Notification Center) got responsive=n/a since they aren't a single app's own responsive layout.

fable: onDismiss is n/a for confirmations, which are half the sample; Discard silently vs Already saved needed a variation for autosaving dialogs.

onDismiss is n/a for half the sample and has no value for autosaving dialogs; Only by completing is ambiguous for confirmations, where Cancel is both a dismissal and an answer; Centered small vs large has no size rule between an alert and a record view.
opus: onDismiss is n/a for half this sample, because confirmations, alerts and viewers hold no work to lose; that is honest but it means the sub-dimension only bites on the five form dialogs. modality is also Blocking almost everywhere — Stacked never appeared and Modeless only in Word — so it discriminates little. The entry has no way to record a deliberate friction like GitHub's type-the-name-to-enable.

onDismiss is the sub-dimension raters could not share: it never says whose work it means — the draft typed inside the dialog, or the work behind it that the dialog is asking about (the TextEdit save sheet) — and it has no value for a surface that commits as you type, which is now the common case. dismissBy's 'Click the backdrop' is really two affordances: clicking a dimmed backdrop, and light-dismissing a dialog that has none (Google Calendar's bubble, Zoom's leave popup); the same conflation shows up as 'Tap the scrim' in bottom-sheet. form and modality also fail together on anchored, scrimless dialogs.
sonnet: onDismiss only makes sense where there's actual draft content at risk; for plain action-confirmations, permission prompts and consent dialogs (about half the sample) I coded n/a rather than force-fit Discard silently, since nothing is being discarded — there was never a draft to lose.

fable: memory is unobservable for admin tables without trying them; two ?s. Page N of M was applied even when M is not shown, since the current page number is.

memory does not say In the URL takes precedence when a URL-paged list also restores on back, which split Amazon and eBay; pageSize is unobservable for infinite feeds (the batch is invisible) and the gloss for Fits the viewport reads as any responsive grid; position has no value for cursor-paged tables that show a count but no range.
opus: pageSize is a system fact rather than something a person can see on any infinite feed — Fixed there means the loader's chunk, which no one experiences; that cell is nearly meaningless for instances 5, 6, 12 and 13. memory is also partly unobservable: whether a feed restores your place varies by session and platform, and I coded the behaviour each product is known for.

memory conflates a mechanism with an outcome: every URL-paged list is also restored on back, so 'In the URL' and 'Restored on back' are not exclusive and the sub wants to be pick any (I kept the address-based code, which is the checkable one). position has no value for a paged collection that shows nothing at all — fable's Count only covers the halfway case, but bare-chevron admin tables (Shopify) fall through entirely. pageSize stays ambiguous between the chunk the system loads and the rows a viewport shows, and it does not care whether the person chooses it on the list or in settings (Gmail).
sonnet: For enterprise dashboards I don't use daily (Stripe, Shopify admin, Google Cloud Console), I inferred Item range and Restored-on-back by common convention for well-built admin tables rather than confirmed personal recall — flagged per-instance rather than marked '?', since I'm reasonably (not fully) confident.

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Mini form: Airbnb — Guests picker under the search bar

fable: Hover cards with one action button (Follow, Add Friend) were coded Read-only preview; Quick actions was reserved for cards whose point is the actions.

Below the anchor and Auto-flip to fit are not exclusive: nearly every web popover is below by default and flips at the viewport edge, so the placement split is about how much a rater knows of the edge case, not the product; dismissBy on touch has no 'release' value and Pointer leaves gets stretched to cover it.
opus: placement came out as Auto-flip to fit for half the sample because modern popover libraries all flip, which makes the variation a statement about the library rather than the design; Beside, with an arrow really means the AppKit look, not a position. Detachable into a window went unused — no instance in this sample can be torn off. contents also forces a choice where a card is a preview with one action in it (GitHub, X, Docs chips).

placement mixes three incompatible things — a side (Below), a behaviour every modern popover library has (Auto-flip), and a platform ornament (Beside, with an arrow) — so an arrowless surface that sits beside its anchor, like a Sheets note or Figma's picker, has nowhere honest to go, and a rater who codes the flip can code almost everything Auto-flip. It should be two subs: habitual side, and whether it flips. persistence and dismissBy also have to agree and the codebook never says so: iOS long-press previews look transient but dismiss like click popovers.
sonnet: Contents was the closest call for hover cards that mix informational content with one action button (GitHub, X, Facebook, Outlook people cards) — I followed the codebook's own precedent of calling the GitHub user card 'Read-only preview' and treated the others the same way for consistency, versus cards where the action is more central (Slack, macOS Mail, Chrome site info), which I coded Quick actions.

values.description: A step explicitly marked as not yet begun or not yet available, distinct from merely being after the current one (GOV.UK task list tags)

values.name: In progress
values.description: A step is explicitly marked as started-but-not-finished, distinct from not yet started, currently active, fully completed, or in error.

fable: states and labels are n/a for plain progress bars, which are a third of the sample; the codebook's form includes bars but its other sub-dimensions assume discrete steps.

form has no value for a vertical rail whose content sits beside it; states and labels need a stated rule for plain progress bars (Current applies, labels do not); rule mixes freedom of movement with dependency, so a branching flow with back holds two values.
opus: Half this sample is a bare progress bar, where labels has nothing to answer (coded n/a) and states collapses to Current — the entry's richer sub-dimensions only bite on the six trails that actually name their steps. Linear, locked and Branching went unused: no instance in the sample forbids going back, and branching is invisible from the stepper itself even in flows that do branch. states also has no variation for Not started, which the GOV.UK task list shows explicitly.

The entry covers two different things under one set of subs: trails with drawn steps, and bare progress bars. For a bar with no divisions, states and labels have nothing to point at and raters split between n/a, an empty answer and 'Current' — the entry should either say those subs are n/a when form is Progress bar only, or give both an explicit none. rule mixes two axes: how freely you may move (locked / back / free) and whether the path branches on your answers, which can be true under any of the first three (Duolingo, TurboTax). form's 'Vertical with content' silently means the Material accordion, leaving the far commoner rail-beside-content vertical stepper with no value.
sonnet: Rule was often an inference rather than confirmed recall for flows I don't use daily (Booking.com, Progressive, Vercel, Indeed) — I defaulted to Linear with back as the common case for consumer setup/checkout flows rather than Linear locked, since most let you revisit earlier answers.

fable: Density is a judgement between Compact and Comfortable for app sidebars; I used Comfortable for roomier sidebars (mail, notes, Notion, Confluence) and Compact for file managers and IDEs.

Arrow keys is a platform fact that raters either know or do not, so it splits every desktop tree; source has no value for groups a person defines (Slack sections) and its Multiple parents gloss reads as being about the items in a node rather than the nodes; Compact vs Comfortable has no measurable line.
opus: source is the sub-dimension that needed the most judgment: I read Authored outline as a hierarchy that exists only in this view (Slack sections, Workflowy bullets, Xcode groups) and Containment as one the tree is reporting from somewhere else. expandBy is also mostly unobservable in the negative — arrow-key expansion exists in nearly every desktop tree whether or not anyone uses it, so those codes describe capability rather than what a person is likely to do.

source is the entry's weak point and it split us on five of twenty instances: Containment, Grouped by attribute and Authored outline are not exclusive in products where the person builds the containment themselves (Notion pages, Confluence pages, Slack custom sections), and the sub-dimension asks what makes one node the parent of another without saying whether the answer is the mechanism or the authorship. Slack in particular is attribute-grouped by default and authored where the person makes a section, so this pick one holds two values. expandBy is the opposite problem: arrow-key expansion exists in nearly every desktop tree whether or not anyone uses it, so a rater who codes capability and a rater who codes observed affordances disagree on almost every instance without disagreeing about the product — it produced sixteen of this entry's thirty-nine cells.
sonnet: Source was the closest call throughout: trees that are literally backed by a filesystem or DOM (Finder, Explorer, Xcode, IntelliJ, GitHub, Obsidian, Figma, registry) got Containment, while trees the person freely drags into an arbitrary parent/child shape without an underlying filesystem (Notion, Confluence, Gmail labels, Workflowy) got Authored outline, even where the codebook's own example (Workflowy) is the only one it names directly.

fable: scale is n/a for booking and poll surfaces that offer no range control. conflicts is n/a for dated to-do lists where items cannot collide. whoseTime for a staff scheduler (one row per employee) was coded Multi-person overlay for want of a 'people as resources' variation.

conflicts as pick any lets [] and n/a both mean nothing happens; the protocol should say which to use when the concept is absent. commitment reads as invite-specific to one rater; its gloss should say it covers any placement that binds.
opus: scale does not apply to booking and poll surfaces at all — Doodle, When2meet and Reminders have no view switch, no zoom and no date jump, coded n/a. conflicts is empty for every project-planning surface because a Gantt has no concept of two things clashing in clock time; that may be worth saying in the codebook rather than leaving raters to guess between an empty array and n/a.

commitment has no value for surfaces where placing something is simply a save — every timeline and to-do got Immediate hold from two of us and n/a from the third, because the variation set is written for invitations.
sonnet: 'commitment' does not really apply to Gantt/task-bar tools (Asana, Project, Notion, Linear, Jira) since editing a bar's dates isn't an RSVP-style binding step the way a calendar invite is; coded n/a rather than force-fitting one of the four event-oriented values.

Three codebook problems surfaced here: (1) 'commitment' has no value for a surface where placing something is simply saved — 'Immediate hold' ('blocks time on create') is calendar-specific and reads oddly for a Gantt bar or a due date, and its gloss should be widened to 'takes effect on save'; (2) 'Allow overlaps' conflates a display treatment (stacked or side-by-side) with a permissive policy, which is what split every rater on the Gantt instances; (3) 'Find a mutual time' is named as a behaviour but glossed as 'search across calendars', which wrongly excludes poll-based products like Doodle. Also: 'whoseTime' has no variation for a project plan, whose time is implied by resource assignment rather than owned by a calendar.

recorded.name: Painted availability grid
recorded.gloss: Participants directly paint their own free time across a continuous grid of days and half-hours; the aggregate renders as a heat map rather than a list of organizer-proposed options

fable: holdBehaviour: 'Timed hold then pay' never applied; booking pages that take a card (Acuity, Square, Resy) confirm on submit rather than holding. constraints for restaurant/class booking is thin because party size, capacity and release windows are not variations.

Pick duration then slot should read service or duration, most booking sites fix length through a service choice. Host-declared windows and Resource inventory overlap for a business whose staff declare hours. Busy blocks visible does not say whose busy blocks.
opus: holdBehaviour's Timed hold then pay never fired: none of these twenty start a countdown on an unpaid reservation (Acuity and Square take payment at booking, which is not the same thing), so that variation may only describe ticketing. availSource blurs for Calendly-likes that both declare windows and subtract connected-calendar busy; I coded the declared windows as the source and noted the subtraction.

constraints is written for host-time rules only, so every inventory booking (tables, classes, seats) has to borrow Working hours or come out empty — the capacity constraint that actually governs those pages has no variation.
sonnet: Group-polling tools (Doodle, When2meet) needed two distinct new slotLayout values since neither matches the four calendar/booking-oriented options; they differ from each other in whether the grid is a fixed set of proposed columns or a freely painted continuum.

Four codebook problems: (1) 'constraints' was read by me in round 1 as what the page displays rather than what rules shrink the slot set, which is what the gloss asks — the gloss should say 'whether or not the booker can see them'; (2) 'slotDisclosure' is a ladder, not a partition — 'Times only' (no host event titles) is true of almost every instance that also carries a price or busy shading, so it wants to be pick any or the gloss needs 'beyond bare times'; (3) 'selectionPath: Pick duration then slot' is really 'pick a service or visit type, which fixes the duration, then a slot' — every clinic, salon and studio booker in this sample takes that shape and none of them ask for a duration as such; (4) 'holdBehaviour' is per-configuration for MyChart, Booksy and Bookings — some visit types or businesses instant-book while others go to a request — so a pick-one forces a false choice. Also: 'availSource' conflates where free/busy comes from (typed windows vs a connected calendar) with what kind of thing is bookable (staff, rooms, seats), which is why Square and Booksy split raters between Host-declared windows and Resource inventory.

fable: inviteFlow and rsvpVisibility are n/a for database/LMS calendars with no invite concept (Notion, Canvas, Moodle, Asana, Trello, Airtable). detailDepth for Outlook desktop follows the single-click peek rather than the codebook's 'Side panel' exemplar.

inviteFlow's Send on save and Optional guests are not exclusive, every calendar here does both. Edit fields only reads as exclusive with drag, so raters who list both make it pick-any-with-a-contradiction. Search events needs to say whether global search counts.
opus: The task-database calendars (Notion, Asana, Trello, Airtable, Canvas, Moodle) have no invitations, so inviteFlow and rsvpVisibility are n/a for six of twenty — the pattern as written assumes a real calendar rather than a date view over records. detailDepth's Inline expand never fired: the codebook names Google Schedule view for it, but on the phone that view opens a full screen, so raters may split on that cell.

moveResize's Edit fields only is glossed 'no direct manipulation', so it is mutually exclusive with Drag to new time — coding it as an additional capability (as I did in round 1) is a trap the pick-any framing invites. inviteFlow's Optional guests is ambiguous between marking a guest optional and guests being optional at all.
sonnet: inviteFlow and rsvpVisibility genuinely don't apply to non-invite calendar surfaces (Notion database, Canvas, Moodle, Asana, Trello, Airtable calendar views) since there is no guest/RSVP concept on a due-date or course-event card; coded n/a rather than force-fitting a value.

Five codebook problems: (1) 'gridFields' mixes two mutually exclusive options ('Title only' vs 'Title and time') into a pick-any, so the array can be self-contradictory — they should be one pick-one sub-dimension or one should be dropped; (2) 'moveResize: Edit fields only' is glossed 'no direct manipulation', which makes it exclusive with Drag and Resize, yet it is the natural place to record 'you can also type the dates' — a separate sub-dimension is needed; (3) 'inviteFlow' is not a partition: Google Calendar is simultaneously Send on save, Optional guests and RSVP required, so this pick-one forces an arbitrary choice and was the hardest cell in the entry; (4) 'detailDepth' cross-cuts anchoring (in place vs dedicated) with depth (summary vs editor), so Moodle's centred modal summary fits Popover summary and Full page or modal equally; (5) the Inline expand exemplar names Google Calendar Schedule view, but on phone that surface pushes a full-screen detail — the exemplar needs a platform. Separately, most of my round-1 pick-any codes were too thin: I coded what a screenshot shows rather than what the surface supports, which the glosses ('pick any that apply') plainly ask for.

fable: chrome is pick-one but List plus timeline and Multi-tier time header co-occur in nearly every tool; I followed the Smartsheet exemplar once and coded the WBS pane otherwise. ganttScale: coded Zoom slider whenever a zoom control exists, the default preset only when there is none.

ganttScale mixes a control (Zoom slider) with default grains (Day, Week, Month); nearly every product has preset zoom levels, so the gloss should say to code the default grain and reserve Zoom slider for a continuous control. Health or status colour and Critical path highlight overlap when critical bars are red.
opus: ganttScale forced a single answer out of products whose timescale is a configurable dropdown (Smartsheet, monday, ClickUp, Airtable): I coded the default the product opens at, reserving Zoom slider for continuous controls, so that column is the least reliable here. rowHierarchy's Grouped by project and Swimlanes by person or team are the same mechanism (group-by) pointed at different fields, which made several cells a coin flip decided by the view's default grouping.

ganttScale is the entry's fault line: Zoom slider is glossed 'continuous', so a Day/Week/Month/Quarter toggle has to be coded as its default scale instead, and one rater coding every zoom control as Zoom slider accounts for most of this entry's disagreement. It needs a 'preset zoom steps' value. barAttrs' Title on bar is the second: in list-plus-timeline schedulers the name is in the table, not on the bar.
sonnet: ganttScale for one product (Notion timeline) got '?' since I couldn't confidently recall whether its zoom is continuous or a set of discrete view steps.

The biggest codebook problem in this entry is 'ganttScale': Day, Week and Month / quarter name the axis grain while Zoom slider names an interaction, so almost every product is both and raters split on whether to code what the axis shows or how it is changed — it should be two sub-dimensions (current grain; scale control: presets vs continuous). 'chrome' has the same fault: List plus timeline and Timeline only describe pane arrangement, Multi-tier time header describes the header, and Compact mobile strip describes a platform, so Smartsheet and GitHub are two of them at once and the pick-one forces a false choice. Third, 'linking' has an explicit 'No links' variation, which makes an empty array ambiguous — the protocol should say that products with no dependencies take ['No links'], not []. Fourth, 'rowHierarchy: Grouped by project' is really 'grouped by any field' and does not cover Asana's grouping by section within one project. Finally, my own round-1 pick-any codes across barAttrs, editGestures and statusFeedback were systematically too thin — I recorded the most salient attribute rather than every one that applies.

Title only in rowFields is exclusive with every other value and should be dropped or glossed as such. timeBinding is pick one but daily planners hold a plan date, a due date and a calendar block at once. Migrate vs Snooze needs a line on postponing overdue items.
opus: itemRichness is the hardest column: most consumer to-do apps sit between Checkbox item and Issue-like task (Todoist and OmniFocus have notes, sub-tasks and comments but still read as checkboxes), so I reserved Issue-like for items with a status workflow and a comment thread and noted it each time. taskStructure also double-fires — Todoist Today is both grouped by date and a saved filter — and I coded the grouping you see rather than the mechanism behind it.
sonnet: Sunsama and Slack Later both populate their lists by importing/saving from elsewhere rather than through any listed createOpen action; coded an empty array rather than force-fitting one.

Codebook problems in this entry: (1) 'rowFields' puts 'Title only' in a pick-any alongside six field names, so any row with a due date makes it self-contradictory — it should be the empty array, or a separate pick-one; (2) 'completionPath: Snooze / defer' and 'Migrate to another day' overlap almost completely — pushing a task to tomorrow is both, and raters split on which name to use for the same gesture; (3) 'timeBinding' is pick-one but Sunsama is genuinely both Time block on calendar and Deadline plus soft plan date, and Things is both Due date only and Deadline plus soft plan date; (4) 'taskStructure' has no value for 'grouped by section within one list', which is Asana's default and Notion's board default; (5) opus's +Save from elsewhere is a real gap — Slack's Later, Google Tasks in Gmail and Sunsama are all populated by capture from another surface rather than by any of the five creation gestures, and I have adopted it for all three.

Query by example: Pinterest — Visual search from a pin

This app: Pinterest — Visual search from a pin

recorded.name: Highlighted in place
recorded.gloss: Matches are highlighted directly within the existing content being searched, with a count, rather than being returned as a separate list of candidate results, e.g. browser Find in page

fable: Initiative as pick-one loses the common pairing of autocomplete with pull; I coded Suggestions while typing wherever autocomplete exists. Instant-results search (Spotify) sits between suggestions and results.

Voice and Natural-language question overlap for every assistant, and Image or camera overlaps Query by example for every visual search. initiative as pick one loses that autocomplete always sits on a pull, and it does not separate query suggestions from instant results. resultForm has no value for a grid of items of one kind (pins, products).
opus: resultForm is the entry's most useful sub because modern engines stack three or four forms on one page, but it has no value for a grid of homogeneous items (Pinterest's pins, an image wall) — I coded those Ranked links, which is a stretch, and no value for in-place matches, which I proposed. initiative is pick-one but the four values are not alternatives: a page can push recommendations before a query, suggest while typing and be pulled, all at once; I coded the behaviour at the moment of searching, which makes 'System pushes' almost uncodeable in a search sample. scope forces a single index on assistants that answer from the device and the web at once (Siri, Windows Search, Spotlight).

Two codebook faults account for most of this entry: `queryForm` mixes modality with form, so Voice and Natural-language question always co-occur and raters split over whether to say both; and `initiative`'s Suggestions-while-typing is glossed with query autocomplete but gets applied to any surface that renders results per keystroke (Spotlight, Windows Search), which is a rendering choice, not who initiated. The find-in-page gap was found by all three raters under three different names.
sonnet: scope is genuinely ambiguous for single-source vertical search tools (PubMed, Scholar, Amazon voice shopping) that are neither the open web nor a general OS/app search; coded as This app by treating the searched database/catalogue itself as the bounded 'app'.

I under-coded the pick-any subs (queryForm, resultForm, refinement) across most of this entry's most heavily-featured products (Google, Bing, ChatGPT, Perplexity, YouTube, Amazon) — naming only the single most distinctive form and missing the several others plainly present, the same pattern I found in the configure archetype's product-configurator entry. Two smaller codebook findings: (1) `queryForm`'s Keywords vs Natural-language question doesn't say whether typing a question into a plain search box counts as the latter, or whether that value is reserved for products designed around question-form input (Perplexity, Siri) — I resolved it the second way, holding DuckDuckGo and Google Scholar to Keywords alone. (2) `resultForm` has no value for 'a grid of homogeneous items that are not links and not a single known entity' (Pinterest's pin grid, Amazon's product tiles) — Ranked links and Entity cards both get stretched to cover this, and all three raters reached for the nearest existing value rather than proposing new ones.

dimensions.name: Facet content
dimensions.question: Which facet types are offered, and how are values shown?

dimensions.name: Facet set
dimensions.question: Where does the set of facets come from?

values.name: Added by the person
values.description: Any attribute can become a facet

dimensions.name: Update model
dimensions.question: When does a facet change take effect?

dimensions.name: Placement
dimensions.question: Where do facets live?

values.name: Modal dialog
values.description: Facets live in a centred dialog over the results on desktop web

dimensions.name: Selection logic
dimensions.question: How do chosen values combine?

dimensions.name: Visual facets
dimensions.question: Are facets drawn, not just listed?

wild.note: Values are chosen by people; which attributes are facets is always decided by the product.

techniques.name: Promote to facet
techniques.how: Any attribute in a result’s detail can be promoted to a facet with computed counts: Fluid Attributes, landed in the facet rail.

techniques.name: Facets from my sentence
techniques.how: A typed need creates the facets and values it implies, each removable.

entries.sample: Retail, travel, real-estate, library and dataset search.
usage: People discover which criteria exist from the facet list itself
questions: Do person-added facets overwhelm the rail, and should they fade with disuse?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Values with counts: Home Depot — Results with left facets

recorded.name: Side drawer
recorded.gloss: Facets slide in as a panel from the screen edge behind a Filters button

recorded.name: Values with a summary metric
recorded.gloss: Each facet value is annotated with an aggregate other than a count — the cheapest price, the best rating, the shortest duration for that value — which tells you what choosing it costs rather than how much it leaves

fable: facetSet is Fixed per category for every instance; the dynamic/added/derived variations did not appear in this sample. Counts beside values are a detail I could not recall for Target.
opus: logic is a constant in this sample: all twenty are OR within, AND across, because that is what a facet rail means; the interesting variations (exclusions, one-value-per-facet) live in advanced library and database search, which this frame barely reaches. facetSet is nearly constant too — every instance is fixed per category — so the two variations that would distinguish research systems (added by the person, derived from the query) go unused; that is a finding about shipping products rather than a coding difficulty. placement's 'Sheet on mobile' had to cover desktop modal filter dialogs (Airbnb, Realtor) because no other value describes a surface laid over the results; the name should lose the 'on mobile'. valueDisplay needed the one proposal: travel search annotates values with prices, not counts.
sonnet: facetSet and logic are near-uniformly Fixed per category / OR within, AND across across this whole sample — every retail, travel and academic search here uses vendor-defined facets combined the standard way; none exhibited dynamic, person-added or query-derived facet sets, so those variations went unused, not because they were hard to apply but because the sample didn't surface them.

entries.name: Recommendations
entries.definition: Items proposed by the system from a person’s behaviour, context or the current item, rather than from a query.

dimensions.name: Basis
dimensions.question: On what grounds is something recommended?

dimensions.name: Rationale
dimensions.question: Does the recommendation say why?

values.name: Explanation on demand
values.example: Facebook Why am I seeing this ad?

dimensions.name: Placement
dimensions.question: Where do recommendations appear?

values.name: Dedicated queue
values.description: A surface whose only content is recommendations, presented one at a time and advanced deliberately (Steam's Discovery Queue, swipe-to-decide apps) — not a shelf inside another screen, not an up-next after content and not a periodic digest

dimensions.name: Steering controls
dimensions.question: How can a person steer?

dimensions.name: Freshness
dimensions.question: How often do recommendations change?

dimensions.name: Nesting
dimensions.question: How are shelves composed?

wild.note: Thumbs and not-interested controls are common; the basis and weighting are never editable.

examples.name: Spotify
examples.note: Exclude a playlist from your taste profile

techniques.name: Steerable shelves
techniques.how: Each shelf exposes its recipe (basis, filters, weights) for editing, forking into a new shelf, and sharing.

techniques.name: Disagree with the reason
techniques.how: A stated reason can be contested (“I watched that for a class”), removing its influence.

techniques.name: More like this, but…
techniques.how: Steer a shelf in words; the change appears as recipe edits.

entries.sample: Streaming, retail, news and app-store home screens.
usage: People keep separate profiles to protect recommendations from shared use
questions: How legible can a recipe be before it stops being a recommendation and becomes a query?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Similar to this item: YouTube — Up next after a video
Context: Facebook — Ad with Why am I seeing this ad

None: YouTube — Up next after a video
Explanation on demand: Facebook — Ad with Why am I seeing this ad

Up next at the end: YouTube — Up next after a video

Not interested: YouTube — Up next after a video
Exclude from taste profile: Amazon — Recommended for you on the home page

Per session: Amazon — Recommended for you on the home page
Live with actions: YouTube — Up next after a video

Single shelf: YouTube — Up next after a video

fable: Placement lacks a variation for a full-screen or single-stream feed that is itself the recommendation (TikTok, Discover, Instagram suggested posts); I used Home shelves. Freshness Per session vs Live with actions is a judgement about recompute timing that is not directly observable.

basis overlaps: Similar to this item and Viewing or purchase history coincide wherever similarity is computed from a history item (Netflix, Amazon, Goodreads), and the raters split on whether to code both. controls' Not interested and Exclude from taste profile have no rule for durable dismissals (Suggest Less, Ignore). placement lacks a value for a feed that is the app's main surface.
opus: rationale hangs on a distinction the codebook leaves implicit: a shelf header that names the evidence ('Because you watched X', 'Because you added X') versus a generic one ('Recommended for you'). I coded the first as Short label and the second as None, and said so per instance; a rater who treats every themed row title as a label would code far more Short labels than I did. placement is written for shelves and has no good home for a recommendation injected into a feed (Instagram, Facebook ads, TikTok's whole surface) — I used Home shelves and flagged each. controls has no None variation, so an empty array means nothing steers it; that is the case for a quarter of the sample. freshness was the least observable sub: whether a shelf recomputes per visit or on a weekly cycle is invisible unless the product says so, and I leaned on what each product advertises.

`rationale` needs its gloss to separate a stated cause ('Because you watched X') from a bare personalisation label ('Picked for you'); that one ambiguity split us on several shelves. `basis` also needs to say whether Similar to this item requires an anchor item on screen or merely item-similarity in the model — I now read it as requiring the anchor, and that rule resolved five of these cells.
sonnet: rationale sometimes shows both a short label and a richer on-demand explanation (12, 19); coded to the richer variation present since pick-one forces a single choice and the on-demand explanation is the more complete disclosure.

Two instances (Amazon n7, Apple Store n9) show I sometimes coded the `placement` sub's canonical example correctly but failed to check whether `nesting` names the same scenario under a different sub — the codebook could flag cross-references between subs that share a worked example. Separately, `controls` disagreements were mostly real gaps in what I'd verified about each product (Amazon n8 contradicted my own note) rather than genuine interpretive splits.

entries.name: Search results
entries.definition: A ranked presentation of items matching a query, with the cues needed to judge relevance and the tools to refine.

dimensions.name: Result representation
dimensions.question: What does a result show, and how is its snippet made?

dimensions.name: Grouping
dimensions.question: Is it one list or many?

values.name: Blended modules
values.description: Videos, maps and stories in one list

values.name: Grouped by type
values.description: Results are sectioned by the kind of thing they are (songs, artists, playlists; applications, documents, mail) in one scroll, rather than split into tabs, blended into a single list or clustered by subject. The archetype entry has this value; this entry does not

dimensions.name: Ranking control
dimensions.question: How much say does the person have in the order?

dimensions.name: Relevance cues
dimensions.question: What helps a person judge a result before opening it?

values.name: Rating and popularity
values.description: The judging signal is a crowd aggregate carried on the result — star rating and review count, downloads, citations, views — which in app, product and scholarly search decides more clicks than the snippet does

dimensions.name: Result preview
dimensions.question: Where does a result open?

dimensions.name: Updating
dimensions.question: When do results change?

wild.note: Some engines let people weight sources or set a region; result representation is fixed.

techniques.name: Result lens
techniques.how: Surface attributes from destination pages (author, date, price, reading time) into every result card: Fluid Attributes across sites.

techniques.name: Personal source weighting
techniques.how: Raise, lower or block a source from its result, visible as an editable list.

techniques.name: Rerank by what I mean
techniques.how: “Prefer primary sources” reranks with a stated rationale shown on each result.

entries.sample: Web engines, retail, scholarly, app-store and in-app search result pages.
entries.unit: One results page for one query.
usage: People open several results in tabs to compare: a composition workaround
questions: When results are generated, what is the overview and what is the detail?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Title, address and snippet: Google — Web results for a query
Summary with citations: Elicit — Results for a research question

Query-biased with highlights: Google — Web results for a query
Generated per result: Elicit — Results for a research question

Blended modules: Google — Web results for a query

Opaque relevance: Google — Web results for a query

Highlighted matches: Google — Web results for a query
Freshness date: Google — Web results for a query
Source identity: Google — Web results for a query

New page: Google — Web results for a query
Side-by-side: Elicit — Results for a research question

On submit: Google — Web results for a query

recorded.name: Grouped by kind
recorded.gloss: Results sectioned by item type (apps, documents, mail) in one list rather than tabs or blended modules

fable: Ranking: Sort by the person coded wherever a sort control exists even if relevance is the default. Snippet is n/a for grids and answer engines whose results carry no text excerpt.

cues lacks the crowd-aggregate cue (stars, downloads, citations, views) that eight of twenty results pages lead with. grouping lacks the archetype's Grouped by type. ranking wants pick any: signed-in engines are both opaque and personalised, and retail pages are both sortable and opaque by default. snippet's n/a for image grids and answer engines is read differently by each rater.
opus: cues needed the bigger of the two proposals: in eight of twenty instances the decisive cue is a crowd aggregate (stars, downloads, citations, views) that the codebook has no name for, while 'Why this matched' went entirely unused — no shipping product in this sample explains its matching. grouping's missing 'grouped by type' is a straight inconsistency with the archetype entry, which has exactly that value in resultForm. ranking's Sort by the person fires whenever a sort control exists, which makes it a fact about the toolbar rather than about the ranking; Opaque relevance and Personalized are almost impossible to tell apart from outside, and I coded Personalized only where the product says it personalises. representation is pick-one but a page like Google's or Bing's carries three representations at once, so I coded the headline one and let the rest fall to grouping.

This entry's low agreement comes from two unstated conventions rather than from the products. First, `snippet` has no rule for a result with no text at all: n/a and Static description were used interchangeably, and I now read Static description as 'text that exists but is not query-built' and n/a as 'no text'. Second, `representation`'s Rich result card is glossed with commerce attributes but gets used for any result denser than a link, which pulled scholarly and media results into it. Two variations are also missing: a grouped-by-kind list (which the archetype already names, so the pattern should inherit it) and a crowd-aggregate cue (ratings, citations, views).
sonnet: ranking came out Opaque relevance for nearly every instance since none of these sampled screens shows an explicit signed-in personalization cue or a person-chosen sort as the default view; Kagi (5) was the one clear exception, matching its own named feature.

The clearest, most consistent miss on my part: whenever a screen has an explicit, visible sort control (Shopping, Amazon, Scholar, Semantic Scholar, Outlook, Slack, YouTube, Zillow), both other raters correctly coded `ranking` as Sort by the person while I defaulted to Opaque relevance across eight separate instances — several of my own notes even named the sort control without the code reflecting it. Two codebook gaps worth recording: (1) `cues` has no value for a crowd-aggregate popularity signal (ratings, downloads, citations, views), which both other raters reached for independently and which I now think is real, adopting opus's +Rating and popularity; (2) `grouping` has no value for content sectioned by kind within one scroll (Spotify's Songs/Artists/Albums/Playlists, Spotlight's Top Hit/Applications/Documents/Mail) — the parent archetype has 'Grouped by type' but this entry's own four values (list/tabs/blended/clustered) can't say it, which both other raters flagged independently with near-identical proposals.

entries.name: Transact and commit
entries.definition: Make a consequential choice, commit to it, and be able to take it back.

dimensions.name: Commit structure
dimensions.question: How many steps stand between choosing and committing?

dimensions.name: Consequence disclosure
dimensions.question: What is said about consequences before committing?

dimensions.name: Reversal
dimensions.question: How can it be taken back?

dimensions.name: Defaults and nudges
dimensions.question: How does the system shape the choice?

values.name: Scarcity pressure
values.description: The choice is shaped by manufactured urgency rather than by a recommendation — only 2 left at this price, 12 other people are looking, this deal ends in 9 minutes

dimensions.name: Unit
dimensions.question: What is being committed to?

wild.note: Saved payment and one-click settings are the only common levers.

techniques.name: Consequence preview
techniques.how: Before committing, a plain list of every effect (charges, notifications, cancellation deadline), each an attribute that can be surfaced into the button itself.

techniques.name: Check this against my rules
techniques.how: Compare a transaction with the person’s stated budget and preferences before commit.

entries.sample: Retail, travel, banking, subscription and government payment flows.
usage: Cost surprises at the last step drive abandonment
questions: Which parts of a transaction may a person customize without weakening consent?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

One-click: App Store — Buying a paid app
Review then confirm: Amazon — Buy Now on a product page

Cost breakdown: Amazon — Buy Now on a product page
Timing estimate: Amazon — Buy Now on a product page
Terms summary: Netflix — Choose a plan and start membership

Cancel within a period: Netflix — Choose a plan and start membership
Return process: Amazon — Buy Now on a product page
App Store — Buying a paid app

Neutral: Amazon — Buy Now on a product page
App Store — Buying a paid app
Recommended option: Netflix — Choose a plan and start membership

One item: Amazon — Buy Now on a product page
App Store — Buying a paid app
A subscription: Netflix — Choose a plan and start membership

fable: unit: coded every P2P payment (Venmo Pay, Zelle, Wise) as One item since a single transfer has one counterparty; the codebook's 'A group transaction' exemplar (Venmo requests) describes splits and requests, which the sample does not locate. Reversal is pick-one, so flows with both a cancel period and returns (Amazon) took the later, longer mechanism.

unit has no value for a transfer to one person; the Venmo exemplar under A group transaction pulls two-party payments into it. nudges lacks scarcity, the commonest travel nudge. Cost breakdown needs a line on whether a single price with plus taxes counts.
opus: unit has no variation for a peer-to-peer payment: the codebook's A group transaction names Venmo, so I used it for Venmo, Zelle and Wise while noting each is two-party. reversal is pick-one but eBay's screen holds two flows at once (a binding bid and a returnable purchase), and most subscriptions are cancel-before-renewal rather than cancel-for-refund, which Cancel within a period only half describes.

unit has no value for a transfer to a person: One item means an item and A group transaction means a split, so Venmo, Zelle and Wise all have to be filed under a name that misdescribes them. Cost breakdown's gloss ('taxes and fees') does not say whether a single stated price counts, which is where most of the disclosure disagreement sits. nudges is pick one but Booking.com truthfully holds both a recommendation label and scarcity pressure — it wants to be pick any.
sonnet: Whether an add-on or trial offer counts as a 'nudge' was often a judgment call; coded Neutral wherever the sample didn't explicitly flag a highlighted, pre-ticked, or personalized option.

Three codebook problems surfaced in reconciliation: (1) disclosure's Cost breakdown gloss ('Taxes and fees') is ambiguous between 'a price is shown' and 'the price is broken into summed components' — a flat subscription price (Netflix, Spotify) split raters until the itemization reading was made explicit; it should be tightened to require multiple components. (2) disclosure's Irreversibility warning got conflated with the separate reversal characteristic more than once (Robinhood, Uber, Wise) — a warning is something said on screen, not an inference from the reversal mechanism, and the gloss should say so explicitly. (3) reversal and unit are pick-one but eBay's Bid-or-Buy-It-Now (irreversible bid vs. return-process purchase) truthfully spans two variations at once, which is a real gap rather than a rater error; nudges also had no variation for manufactured scarcity/urgency (Booking.com's 'only 2 left'), which +Scarcity pressure now covers.

entries.name: Approval flow
entries.definition: Routing a request to people who approve it, reject it or ask for changes.

dimensions.name: Routing
dimensions.question: Who reviews, in what order?

dimensions.name: Review surface
dimensions.question: What does a reviewer see?

dimensions.name: Decision actions
dimensions.question: How is a decision made?

dimensions.name: Timing
dimensions.question: What if nobody decides?

dimensions.name: Visibility
dimensions.question: Who sees the discussion and history?

dimensions.name: Status to requester
dimensions.question: What does the requester see while waiting?

wild.note: Rules are configured by administrators, not by the people reviewing.

techniques.name: Decide where you are
techniques.how: Approve from any surface (email, chat, a notification) with the key attributes surfaced into that surface, Fluid Attributes into the notification.

techniques.name: Summarize risk
techniques.how: A summary of the request’s risks and policy exceptions, each linked to evidence.

entries.sample: Code review, expense, procurement, HR and content publishing tools.
usage: Reviewers rubber-stamp when the surface lacks evidence
questions: What must a reviewer always see, whatever they customize?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: timing was hard to code from product knowledge: whether reminders or escalation are default versus admin-configured is not visible to a requester, so Reminders/Escalation for enterprise tools (Coupa, ServiceNow, Ariba) is moderate confidence.

Request summary reads as either the request's own description (every tool) or a summary-as-primary-surface (expense tools); the gloss should say. Sequential chain and Conditional by rule overlap when rules generate a chain. Who is holding it and Stage by stage overlap whenever a chain shows the current holder.
opus: actions needed a Hold or Send-back-without-rejecting value for Coupa and Concur — I folded send-back into Request changes and left Hold uncoded. routing's Parallel reviewers and Conditional by rule overlap badly: GitLab, Azure DevOps and ServiceNow all compute a parallel reviewer set from rules, and I split them by whether a human names the reviewers (parallel) or a rule does (conditional), which is a judgement another rater could easily make the other way.

status is pick one but Expensify, DocuSign, Ariba and Teams all truthfully show both the stage and the person holding it — it wants to be pick any. Parallel reviewers conflates two things, several reviewers at once and a rule that they must approve, which is what made Figma and Azure DevOps split three ways. Delegate and Approve from a notification also sit oddly in 'Decision actions': one is an out-of-band configuration, the other a surface, and neither is a decision.
sonnet: timing (deadline/escalation behavior) was often not directly evident from the sample note and inferred from general knowledge of each product category (finance/procurement tools escalate, lightweight dev/task tools don't); flagged the more confident cases only where the note said so explicitly.

Two codebook problems recurred here. (1) visibility's Comments on items and Full audit trail are not mutually exclusive in review tools with inline diff/document commenting plus a separate history record (GitLab, Gerrit, Google Docs, DocuSign, Figma) — several of my round-1 codes picked the wrong one of two things that were both present, which the pick-one framing hides; DocuSign and Google Docs genuinely have both, and only their relative prominence separates them. (2) status's three variations (Final result only / Stage by stage / Who is holding it) collapse toward each other whenever routing is Single approver: naming 'who is holding it' is trivial when there is exactly one possible holder, which produced repeated three-way splits (BambooHR, Asana, Figma) that a scope note tying status readings to routing structure would resolve.

usage: Flexible travellers compare across dates before choosing any
questions: Is an availability grid an overview whose items are time slots?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Date first: Booking.com — Hotel search and room selection
Flexible across dates: Google Flights — Flight search and select
Hopper — Flight booking with price prediction

List of slots: Booking.com — Hotel search and room selection
Price calendar: Google Flights — Flight search and select
Hopper — Flight booking with price prediction

No hold: Google Flights — Flight search and select

Price per option: Google Flights — Flight search and select
Few left: Booking.com — Hotel search and room selection
Demand level: Booking.com — Hotel search and room selection
Price change warning: Google Flights — Flight search and select
Hopper — Flight booking with price prediction

Party size: Google Flights — Flight search and select
Several units: Booking.com — Hotel search and room selection

Email and calendar invite: Booking.com — Hotel search and room selection

fable: confirmation: 'Email and calendar invite' was used for every emailed confirmation even where no .ics is attached, since there is no plain 'Email' variation; ticketing coded Wallet pass because the pass is the artifact. Google Flights has no confirmation of its own (n/a).

Party size and Several units are not distinguishable for ticket quantity. Wallet pass names a boarding pass, which arrives at check-in, not at booking; the gloss should say which moment it codes. Sonnet coded n/a for confirmation on screens before purchase, so the unit of analysis needs to say the flow is coded through to its end.
opus: confirmation is pick-one but nearly every flow confirms on screen, emails a record and offers a pass; I coded the durable artefact the product pushes you toward (wallet pass for travel and ticketing, email for hotels and restaurants) rather than the on-screen page, which is the choice most likely to split raters. signals and extras are empty for all four clinic/health bookings, which is itself a finding: medical booking flows deliberately carry no price, scarcity or upsell.

confirmation is pick one but every flow here also confirms on screen, so On screen is a floor that competes with the artefact that actually matters — it wants to be pick any, or to be re-glossed as 'the durable artefact'. order has no value for a flow whose date and venue are both fixed by the item (Eventbrite, any single event), which is what sent three raters to three different codes. signals lacks a value rating — SeatGeek's Deal Score is a judgement about price against market, not a demand level, and I coded it Demand level only because nothing else fits. Party size and Several units also overlap wherever a quantity picker both counts the party and adds units.
sonnet: confirmation is n/a for several instances (Google Flights, Southwest, Hopper, Ticketmaster/SeatGeek/StubHub seat maps, AMC) because the sampled screen is search/selection prior to an actual completed booking, which happens on a later screen not described here.

Two codebook problems recurred here. (1) order has no variation for a booking flow entered at a single already-fixed event/venue+time where the remaining choice is only ticket type and quantity (Eventbrite) — none of the four variations describe that, and n/a is a real gap rather than a rater disagreement. (2) confirmation and the entry's stated 'unit of analysis: one booking flow' pulled against the literal 'screen' sample text more than once: several of my round-1 n/a codes wrongly stopped coding at the pictured pre-purchase screen (Southwest's calendar, Ticketmaster's seat map, Hopper's price-prediction view) instead of coding the whole flow's eventual confirmation from product knowledge, the way fable and opus did — the codebook could say explicitly whether a sampled screen bounds the instance or merely anchors it.
