entries.name: Checkout
entries.definition: The flow that turns a cart into a paid order: contact, delivery, payment and review.

dimensions.name: Structure
dimensions.question: How is the flow divided?

dimensions.name: Order summary
dimensions.question: How visible is what is being bought?

dimensions.name: Prefill
dimensions.question: What arrives filled in?

dimensions.name: Cost disclosure
dimensions.question: When is the full cost known?

dimensions.name: Payment options
dimensions.question: How are ways to pay offered?

dimensions.name: Abandonment
dimensions.question: What happens when a person leaves?

wild.note: Checkouts are optimized by the merchant and never customizable.

techniques.name: Express, expandable
techniques.how: A one-tap path for returning buyers where every step can be expanded in place to check or change it.

entries.sample: Top retail, travel and ticketing checkouts.
usage: Buyers re-open the summary to check totals before paying
questions: Is a checkout the rare pattern where malleability should stay low?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

fable: structure's 'Guest or account' and 'Express wallet' are orthogonal to page shape, so I coded page shape and noted the gate/express buttons. abandonment: 'Synced across devices' whenever the cart lives on an account, 'Saved cart' for cookie carts, 'Reminder' where recovery emails are the product's known behaviour.

structure mixes how pages divide with the guest-or-account entry fork, which nearly every retail checkout has; Guest or account should be its own sub. Everything up front vs Running total needs a rule for totals that move with shipping and tips. abandonment is pick one but signed-in carts are saved, synced and reminded at once.

Three sub-dimensions cannot be applied consistently as written. abandonment: Saved cart and Synced across devices nest rather than exclude each other (every synced cart is a saved cart; the codebook's Saved cart exemplar is Amazon while Synced's gloss 'signed-in carts' describes Amazon), and Reminder is orthogonal to both, so a signed-in cart with recovery emails holds three values of a pick-one sub; the remaining disagreement there (Zara, and sonnet's Saved cart on the delivery apps) is raters choosing how strong a claim to make, not different readings of the product, and it will not converge until Synced is either folded into Saved cart or the sub becomes pick any. prefill: Address autocomplete is a typing aid, not something that arrives filled in, so it nests inside Blank rather than being an alternative to it; the sub conflates initial state with entry assistance. disclosure: Everything up front versus Running total with estimates has no rule for totals that move with in-flow choices (delivery speed, tip, fulfilment), so the boundary sits wherever each rater draws it and Everything up front collapses to option-free pages. payment: Pay later is glossed by Klarna but its name also covers pay-at-property timing and store-card financing, and Wallet buttons conflates a wallet as a tender in a list with a wallet as an express button; tenders (miles, EBT, gift cards) have no code.
opus: structure is pick-one but Guest or account is a different axis from Multi-page / One page / Express wallet — almost every checkout here is both (guest choice and a page count), so I coded Guest or account only where the first screen is literally that fork, and raters could easily code Amazon or Etsy the other way. prefill is similarly layered: a signed-in Shopify checkout is wallet autofill, saved details and address autocomplete at once.

structure mixes two axes and a special case: Multi-page steps and One page answer 'how is the flow divided', while Guest or account is an identity question true of nearly every instance and Express wallet is a path through the flow rather than a division of it — that is most of this entry's disagreement. abandonment is a nesting, not a partition: Nothing kept is inside Saved cart is inside Synced across devices, Reminder is orthogonal to all three, and the codebook names Amazon under Saved cart while glossing Synced as 'signed-in carts'. Pay later covers BNPL, pay-at-property and store-card financing at once, and the payment sub-dimension names payment surfaces so alternative tenders (EBT, miles, points, store credit) cannot be coded at all.

Three defects account for all 17 cells, and two of them are the kind that cannot be reconciled by re-reading the product. (1) abandonment is a nesting plus an orthogonal, not a partition: Nothing kept ⊂ Saved cart ⊂ Synced across devices are the same claim at increasing strength, so a rater's confidence — not the product — decides the code, while Reminder answers a separate question (outreach, not persistence) and Etsy, Amazon and SHEIN are truthfully both; 6 of the 17 cells are this, and I regard the sub-dimension as unreliable as written rather than mis-applied. It needs splitting into a persistence scale (nothing / this device / the account) and a separate yes-no for reminders, and its own gloss contradicts itself by naming Amazon under Saved cart while glossing Synced as 'signed-in carts'. (2) prefill conflates what arrives filled with what helps you fill: Address autocomplete is not an alternative to Blank, it nests inside it, so n20 has two true codes under pick one — it wants pick any, or Address autocomplete moved to an input-assist sub-dimension. (3) disclosure conflates timing with finality: Everything up front vs Running total with estimates asks both 'is the total there from the start' and 'is it final', and Amazon is yes to the first and no to the second (n1). Two further notes that are naming, not structure: Pay later is named for deferred payment and glossed for BNPL financing, and the two sets differ (n16); and payment names surfaces only, so EBT, miles, points and store credit — on screen at Instacart and Delta — cannot be coded at all. Finally, a process observation: at least 5 of these cells (n4, n5, n15, n9, n16) are raters swapping positions between rounds and citing each other's abandoned codes as support, which inflates the apparent disagreement on structure.
sonnet: abandonment behavior for on-demand food delivery apps (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Instacart) was marked '?': restaurant/shopper availability is time-sensitive so I'm not confident whether an abandoned cart is saved, reminded, or simply dropped.

Two codebook problems, one of them large. (1) structure's four values conflate two different axes: three of them (Multi-page steps / One page / Express wallet) describe how many pages the flow spans, while the fourth (Guest or account) describes who must sign in — a question most real checkouts answer independently of their page count (Amazon is both One page and lets you check out as guest-or-account). My round-1 codes defaulted to Guest or account almost everywhere the choice was visible on screen, which is a real miss, but the deeper issue is that this pick-one sub-dimension is answering two different questions with one value; per the reconciliation rule I took the step-shape value since the codebook lists it first and it's what 'How is the flow divided?' is actually asking, but nearly every instance here also truthfully has a guest-or-account choice that the codebook currently has no room to also record. (2) disclosure's Running total with estimates and Everything up front collapsed into each other constantly: almost any checkout that shows a total early but lets one more input (a delivery slot, a coupon, a tip) still adjust it got split three ways, because the codebook doesn't say how much a total needs to move for 'running' to apply versus 'up front' meaning the number is right the first time. Ticketmaster (n14) was the interesting exception — a specific, dated regulatory fact (the FTC's 2025 all-in-pricing rule) changed which value is actually correct now, which is a case worth flagging as a place where a codebook exemplar can go stale rather than being wrong.

The abandonment sub-dimension cannot be applied consistently as pick-one, and I agree with both other raters' diagnosis: Nothing kept, Saved cart and Synced across devices are not parallel alternatives but three strengths of a single underlying claim (a synced cart is definitionally also a saved cart, which is definitionally not 'nothing kept'), while Reminder names an unrelated axis - an outbound notification - that coexists with any of the other three (Etsy does both, per fable's own n7 note; Amazon is the codebook's own Saved cart exemplar while also matching its Synced gloss, 'signed-in carts', a clash opus named at n1 in round 2). Every abandonment disagreement in this packet (n7, n9, n11, n12, n13, n18) reduces to raters choosing a different confidence level on the same underlying fact, not seeing different products - exactly the failure mode described going into this round. I'm holding my codes at n7/n11/n12/n13 (weaker, more defensible tier), and at n9/n18 I already sit with the majority (also worth noting neither of those was a case of me converging to reach that agreement - n9 and n18 already matched fable and opus respectively going into this round). Two smaller findings from the other recoded cells: (1) structure's 'how many steps' question is ambiguous about whether a modal/sheet used to edit one field counts as a step; I now read the codebook's own One page exemplar (Shopify, which itself has edit sheets) as settling this toward 'no', and moved Walmart/Target/Expedia (n4, n5, n15) to One page on that basis rather than by deferring to the other raters' count. (2) payment's Pay later is glossed only by Klarna-style BNPL financing, but real products use the phrase 'pay later' for plain charge-timing choices too (Booking.com's pay-at-property, n16); I held these apart since the underlying UI mechanism differs even where the marketing word matches, but the gloss doesn't say so explicitly.

entries.name: Plan picker
entries.definition: Presenting tiers of a product or subscription to choose among.

dimensions.name: Presentation
dimensions.question: How are tiers arranged?

values.name: Stacked list
values.description: Tiers as a vertical list of rows with a radio or tap target, one line each, with no side-by-side columns or feature table (mobile upgrade sheets)

dimensions.name: Feature disclosure
dimensions.question: How are features compared?

dimensions.name: Recommendation
dimensions.question: Does the page steer?

dimensions.name: Price framing
dimensions.question: How is price expressed?

dimensions.name: Commitment
dimensions.question: What does choosing commit to?

wild.note: Pricing pages are fixed marketing surfaces.

techniques.name: Price for my usage
techniques.how: Enter your actual usage and every tier recomputes a real price and fit.

techniques.name: Which plan fits me?
techniques.how: An answer built from the person’s usage, showing the features it relied on.

entries.sample: SaaS, streaming, mobile carrier and cloud pricing pages.
usage: Buyers skip marketing highlights and scroll to the matrix
questions: Is a plan picker a comparison table the seller controls?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Contract: Adobe Creative Cloud — Plans and pricing

fable: recommendation ('Most popular' badges) is the least stable thing on a pricing page and several codes are moderate confidence (Notion, Dropbox, Verizon). commitment is n/a for a calculator that sells nothing.

presentation's Comparison table and disclosure's Full matrix below describe the same table from two sides, so raters split on which sub it belongs to. commitment's Upgrade now and Change any time are both true of every monthly SaaS plan. Local currency needs a gloss: localized regional pricing, or any price in the visitor's currency.
opus: presentation and disclosure collapse into each other whenever the tiers are drawn as a comparison table (Netflix, Duolingo): the table is both the arrangement and the feature comparison, so Full matrix below is technically wrong — the matrix is not below anything. framing has no value for an add-on priced separately from the tier (Notion AI, Verizon perks, Copilot), which came up repeatedly.

presentation and disclosure overlap: cards with a matrix beneath can be coded as either Tier cards side by side or Comparison table, and only reading disclosure's Full matrix below settles it — the two sub-dimensions need a sentence saying which one owns the table. Most popular highlight has no threshold, so an explicit badge and mere visual prominence get the same code. commitment mixes the CTA (Upgrade now, Free trial) with the term (Change any time, Contract), so almost every monthly SaaS plan truthfully holds two values. Local currency reads as either 'the price is regional' or 'the page offers a currency control', which split every consumer instance three ways.
sonnet: recommendation was 'None' for most enterprise SaaS pricing pages sampled, since the specific screen notes didn't call out a most-popular badge even though many such pages do have one in reality — coded strictly from what the sample and my recall together support rather than assuming every pricing page highlights a tier.

Two codebook problems. (1) commitment's Upgrade now and Change any time collapse together for almost any SaaS plan that charges immediately with no trial but is also cancelable month to month (Notion, Figma, Zoom, GitHub, iCloud+, Google One) — nearly every instance without a trial gate truthfully holds both, and the tie-break (take the first-listed value that applies) mechanically favors Upgrade now every time, which may not be what the sub-dimension is meant to capture; it would help to scope Upgrade now specifically to app-store-style in-app-purchase mechanics rather than any immediate-charge web purchase. (2) presentation's Tier cards side by side has no room for a vertical single-column mobile list (YouTube, iCloud+, Google One) that is neither side-by-side cards nor a shared-row table — fable's proposed +Stacked list fills a real gap, and I adopted it. Separately (not a codebook problem, my own round-1 error): I had repeatedly coded presentation as Comparison table for any page that also showed a feature matrix somewhere on it, when the primary visual unit was actually highlighted cards with a matrix underneath (Slack, Figma, Zoom, GitHub, ChatGPT, Adobe) — Comparison table should be reserved for pages where tiers are literally columns of one shared table from the start (Netflix), which is a narrower case than I was applying it to.

entries.name: Confirmation
entries.definition: A deliberate pause asking a person to confirm a consequential action.

dimensions.name: Friction
dimensions.question: How much effort does confirming take?

values.name: Swipe to confirm
values.description: A slider or swipe gesture commits the action, so it cannot be triggered by a stray tap

values.name: Physical button plus biometric
values.description: A hardware button press (double-click the side button) combined with Face ID or Touch ID authorises the action
values.example: Apple Pay — Confirm with side button

values.name: Biometric confirm
values.description: Confirming means authenticating — Face ID, a fingerprint, a hardware button press — rather than pressing a button in the interface; the proof of intent comes from the device
values.example: Apple Pay — Confirm with side button

values.name: Re-authenticate
values.description: Confirming requires proving who you are again — re-entering the password or a 2FA code — rather than typing the object's name

dimensions.name: Explanation
dimensions.question: What does it explain?

dimensions.name: When to ask
dimensions.question: Under what conditions does it appear?

values.name: On a likely mistake
values.description: The dialog appears only when a heuristic suggests a slip (empty subject, 'attached' with no attachment), not on every action or only irreversible ones

values.name: On a detected condition
values.description: The dialog appears only because the system noticed something specific about this particular action (an empty subject line, unsaved changes, a mentioned attachment that is missing) — not because the action is always dangerous

dimensions.name: Form
dimensions.question: Where does it ask?

wild.note: Don’t ask again checkboxes let people remove some confirmations.

examples.name: macOS
examples.note: Warn before emptying the Trash setting

techniques.name: Undo over asking
techniques.how: A person chooses an undo window instead of a confirmation for a class of actions.

entries.sample: Destructive and financial actions across apps.
usage: Habitual confirmation clicks defeat the dialog
questions: Which confirmations survive once undo is universal?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Physical button plus biometric: Apple Pay — Confirm with side button

On a detected condition: Microsoft Word — Save changes on close

recorded.name: Slide to confirm
recorded.gloss: The commit requires dragging a control across a track (swipe up to submit, slide to power off): deliberate and hard to do by accident, like hold-to-confirm but a different gesture

fable: friction: I read 'Consequence in the button' as any verb-labelled button (Delete, Send money, Empty Trash) and 'Simple confirm' as OK/Yes/No; the codebook's 'Delete 3 files' example may intend a stricter reading (count in the label), which would move most of these to Simple confirm.

Consequence in the button needs a line on whether a bare verb (Delete) counts or only a button that names the outcome (Delete 3 files, Empty Trash); raters split on exactly that. Sheets read as Modal to two raters and Popover to one; say that action sheets are modal.
opus: friction as written only covers button-shaped confirmations; three of twenty commit through a gesture or an identity check instead, hence the proposals. Consequence in the button versus Simple confirm also needs a rule — I read the button text alone (Empty Trash and Delete forever name the consequence; a bare Delete does not) and noted it, but a rater reading the whole dialog would code several of these differently.

friction has no threshold between Simple confirm and Consequence in the button: fable counted every verb-labelled button, sonnet and I only buttons that name the object or its permanence, and that one reading accounts for most of this entry's disagreement — the gloss's own example ('Delete 3 files') should be made the test. friction also has no value for confirming by authenticating: Apple Pay's side-button-plus-Face-ID and Facebook's password re-entry are the same move and produced three different codes between us. explanation's What will happen is glossed 'Most', which makes it either always true or a residual category, and raters split on whether a permanence warning replaces it. when cannot separate Always from Only irreversible actions for an action that is always irreversible.
sonnet: Gmail's missing-subject warning is the one case where 'when' didn't fit any of the four listed values, since it fires on a specific content condition rather than always/irreversible-only/above-a-threshold/never.

Three findings. (1) friction's Simple confirm and Consequence in the button kept splitting on how specific a button's label has to be: a bare repeated verb (Delete, Pay, Send money, Refund) versus a button that names a scoped outcome (Empty Trash, Delete Photo, Delete forever, Save/Don't Save) — the codebook's own gloss example ('Delete 3 files') implies the latter, but nothing states the threshold explicitly, and I initially coded almost everything as Simple confirm by treating any action-verb button as generic. (2) Two raters independently proposed near-identical friction variations under different names for the same mechanics — 'Swipe to confirm' (fable, sonnet) vs 'Slide to confirm' (opus) for n11/n12, and 'Physical button plus biometric' (fable) vs 'Biometric confirm' (opus) for n10 — which is a coordination gap worth a codebook line rather than three separate proposals surviving to compete. (3) form's Modal and Popover collapsed for any iOS/mobile bottom sheet or action sheet across four instances (n3, n6, n10, n14); Popover's own gloss example is a small anchored Popconfirm-style callout, a narrower pattern than a full-width blocking sheet, and I was applying it too broadly to anything that wasn't a centered desktop dialog box.

entries.name: Undo
entries.definition: Reversing recent actions.

dimensions.name: Unit
dimensions.question: What can be undone?

dimensions.name: Access
dimensions.question: How is it triggered?

values.name: Multi-finger gesture
values.description: A touch gesture such as a two-finger tap or three-finger swipe triggers undo, distinct from shaking the device
values.example: Apple Notes — Shake to undo on iPhone

values.name: Context menu on the item
values.description: Undo is offered in the long-press or right-click menu of the thing just acted on, not globally

values.name: Touch gesture
values.description: A multi-finger tap or swipe on the canvas or page undoes, with no button, shortcut or toast involved (Procreate's two-finger tap, iOS three-finger swipe)
values.example: Apple Notes — Shake to undo on iPhone

values.name: Context menu on the object
values.description: Undo is reached by long-pressing or right-clicking the affected object itself — the sent message, the moved file — rather than from any global undo control

dimensions.name: Window
dimensions.question: How long is undo possible?

dimensions.name: Multiple people
dimensions.question: Whose actions are undone?

dimensions.name: Preview
dimensions.question: Does it say what will be undone?

values.name: Named action
values.example: Undo Typing in macOS Edit menu

wild.note: Undo windows and history depth are occasionally settings.

techniques.name: Named history
techniques.how: The undo stack is visible, named and selectively reversible.

entries.sample: Editors, email, design and file management.
usage: People undo to see what an action did, then redo
questions: Does a malleable interface need undo for customizations as well as content?

coding.protocol: Shared sample of recalled instances; three model raters coded independently; Fleiss’ κ per sub-dimension, item-weighted per entry; disagreements sent back for reconciliation; majority consensus.

Last action only: Asana — Undo after completing a task
Many levels: Google Docs — Undo and version history
Figma — Undo in a shared file

Keyboard shortcut: Google Docs — Undo and version history
Figma — Undo in a shared file
Toolbar button: Google Docs — Undo and version history
Apple Notes — Shake to undo on iPhone
Shake: Apple Notes — Shake to undo on iPhone
History panel: Google Docs — Undo and version history
Figma — Undo in a shared file
Touch gesture: Apple Notes — Shake to undo on iPhone

Session: Figma — Undo in a shared file
Seconds: Asana — Undo after completing a task
Version history: Google Docs — Undo and version history

Only my own changes: Google Docs — Undo and version history
Figma — Undo in a shared file

No: Google Docs — Undo and version history
Figma — Undo in a shared file
Named action: Apple Notes — Shake to undo on iPhone

recorded.name: Multi-finger tap gesture
recorded.gloss: A tap gesture using two or more fingers on the canvas directly triggers undo (or redo), distinct from a shake, a toolbar button, a keyboard shortcut, or a history panel

recorded.name: Long-press context menu
recorded.gloss: Holding down on the specific item to be undone reveals a context menu with an Undo/recall action, rather than an automatic toast, a persistent toolbar button, a shortcut, or a history panel

fable: window: coded 'Version history' only where the product's version history is part of the sample's description (Docs, Figma, Canva, VS Code), 'Session' for other editors even when they also keep versions (Word/OneDrive). preview: toasts that name the action ('Task completed - Undo') were read as Named action.

window's Version history exemplar (Docs) is a recovery mechanism apart from the undo stack, so raters cannot tell whether the sub codes the stack or any recovery. preview is pick one but a product's shortcut and its toast differ. Seconds has no room for a two-minute recall.
opus: window's three values do not fit cleanly: iMessage's two minutes is neither seconds nor version history, and several editors (VS Code, Vim, Canva) have a session stack and a separate long-term recovery store at once, so I coded the undo stack and noted the other. unit's Per-object history never fired — the codebook names Figma for it, but Figma's Cmd+Z is an ordinary per-user linear stack, which is worth checking before round two.

window (and with it unit and preview) assumes one undo mechanism per product, but Docs, Figma, VS Code and Canva each have a session stack and a version history with different answers, so a rater has to decide which mechanism the entry is about before coding anything — that choice, not the products, is what split us. preview does not distinguish naming the action beforehand from reporting it afterwards, which is what Vim exposes. Single-user stack is glossed 'Desktop apps' but reads as 'there is no stack shared with anyone', so collaborative products with a private stack can be coded either way. access has no value for a menu item — Finder's Edit menu, Explorer's context menu, iMessage's long-press menu are all coded as toolbar buttons or as proposals.
sonnet: Several tools (VS Code, Canva) blur session-scoped undo with a separate, longer-lived version-history feature; coded the more persistent/distinguishing value (Version history) where the sample named it explicitly.

Two codebook problems and one of my own recurring errors. (1) unit's Many levels and Jump to a past state collapse together whenever a tool combines an everyday step-back stack with a separate way to jump straight to a named/timestamped point (Google Docs' version history, Word's undo dropdown) — both genuinely apply at once, and the tie-break (take the first-listed value) mechanically favors Many levels, which is worth a codebook note rather than treating each case as a fresh disagreement. (2) Two pairs of raters proposed near-identical new access variations under different names for the same mechanic (touch gestures: fable's 'Multi-finger gesture' / opus's 'Touch gesture' / my own 'Multi-finger tap gesture'; context-menu recall: fable's 'Context menu on the item' / opus's 'Context menu on the object' / my own 'Long-press context menu') — a real coordination gap where the finding was right three times over but the naming never converged, which cost real signal in the kappa calculation. (3) My own recurring error, not a codebook gap: for window and multiUser I had judged case by case whether a tool's separate version-history feature or shared-editing context was 'central enough' to count, and did so inconsistently across genuinely similar products (Figma vs VS Code vs Canva) — on reconciliation I applied one consistent rule (the undo command's own stack is session-bound; a separate snapshot/history feature doesn't change that; a shared/collaborative editing context makes multiUser Only my own changes) across all three instead of judging each on a vibe.
